Last week an old woman posted that her gas cylinder was empty, and Xiaowen answered three hours late. At the shop you talk to customers better than anyone.”

    “…Oh.”

    “We really are short of people.”

    “Oh,” said Su Tang again, and this time her voice brightened. “Then I need to ask my mum and dad! Wait a sec! Just a sec!”

    She put the phone down on the washbasin and ran out. Ye Zhixing heard the toilet door open and close, someone singing on the TV outside, a little boy shouting “Sis, are you done yet,” Su Tang shouting “No!”, and then her talking to someone, through the door, too muffled to make out.

    Seven or eight minutes later she came back, a little out of breath.

    “My dad says signing a contract is a good thing,” she said. “He says before I sign, send him the contract, he wants to read it clause by clause. Sorry, he’s like that, he reads the whole manual when he buys a rice cooker.”

    “He should.”

    “My mum says…” Su Tang paused, as if choosing which part she could say. “My mum says it’s better than waiting tables somewhere. And then she said again that I still have to go to teachers’ college.” She laughed first. “She’s been going on all day. Their mill has stopped work, they only pay the minimum wage now, and my dad’s factory is about the same. The auntie downstairs from us works at the tax bureau, she’s been at home every day, and her wages haven’t lost a cent. So my mum says, see, see, people with a permanent government post.”

    “Mm.”

    “She’s not complaining,” Su Tang said at once. “She’s just… saying. My mum and dad are fine, their social insurance is all paid up, they just haven’t got a permanent post.”

    “I know.”

    That evening, Ye Zhixing sent the contract over. A little after nine, Su Tang sent a photo: under the light in her living room, her dad in reading glasses, holding the phone far away, a pencil in his other hand, making notes on a sheet of white paper. On the paper was written “Party A”, “Party B”, “probation period?”, “Clause 7 confidentiality what does it mean”.

    Then one line after it: he’s been reading it for forty minutes.

    Half an hour later:

    my dad says its fine!! he says the contracts very properly written, he says your companys a proper company
    he also asked how old you are
    i said sixteen
    he went quiet for ages
    then he said the young will surpass us
    im dying

    He called Gu Xuerong twice.

    The first time nobody answered. He knew she didn’t necessarily look at her phone in the daytime, and the signal in the basement was bad. The second time it rang five times, and she answered.

    “Hello.”

    “That game from this afternoon,” he said. “I’ve decided to do it.”

    He went through what had been said at the meeting: a mini-game, Rice Cake, catching cat treats, Big Liu, Cocos, revive by rewarded video. When he got to the word “testing,” he put it another way.

    “We need someone to test. That means playing the game over and over, finding what’s wrong with it, writing it down. Remote, you can do it from where you are. Your cat café contract moves to the company, and from now on instead of the accounts, you do this.”

    There was no sound at the other end.

    “Two thousand five hundred a month.”

    Still no sound. He heard the compressor of the little fridge in her basement start up with a hum.

    “Testing,” said Gu Xuerong, “how much does it usually pay.”

    He hadn’t expected her to ask that first.

    “If you outsource it, it’s by the person-day,” he told her honestly. “One person, one day, two or three hundred. If you count ten days a month—”

    “Two thousand five hundred is cheap.”

    “It is cheap.”

    “Then I’m cheap.”

    “You’re cheap.”

    She went quiet again, not for long this time.

    “OK,” she said.

    Then she said: “Don’t pay my wages into my card.”

    “Why not?”

    “My dad took me to open the card,” she said. “In middle school, when the school wanted fees paid, he took me. It has his phone number on it. When money goes into the card, his phone rings.”

    Ye Zhixing said nothing, waiting for her to go on.

    “He’d come and ask for it.”

    “He would,” said Gu Xuerong. “He owes people money.”

    Ye Zhixing didn’t ask how much, or who to. He said they’d use WeChat for now, and he’d ask Uncle He about the bank.

    When he’d hung up, he sent Uncle He a message. Uncle He replied twenty minutes later:

    Over sixteen, with a labour contract and proof of income, she can go to the bank with her own ID and open one herself, no guardian needed.
    When the banks open, I’ll take her.
    The new card will have her own number on it.

    He forwarded it to Gu Xuerong unchanged.

    She replied with one word: “OK.”

    5. Enzyme Drink

    A little after eleven at night, Su Tang’s phone was charged, and she got on MC.

    Gu Xuerong was already in. She wasn’t building; she was putting up a fence beside the little wooden house by the river, setting the posts one by one, enclosing a neat square of ground with three sheep shut inside.

    “What are you doing?”

    “Penning sheep.”

    “Why pen sheep?”

    “The last ones ran off,” said Gu Xuerong. “Beds need wool. We’ll need more.”

    Su Tang said “oh,” got out some wooden fence posts too, and helped set them beside her. As she set them, she started talking. When she talked her hands usually didn’t stop, the same as when she brushed cats at the shop while chatting to customers.

    She said she’d got her charger back off Su Yu, and Su Yu had cried, and when he’d finished crying he’d come running over wanting her to pick him up. She said her dad had read the contract for over an hour, and after he’d finished he was still in the living room telling her mum “the young will surpass us,” and her mum had asked him what it meant, and he had explained for ages, and her mum had said oh, and gone back to her TV drama. She said her bigger little brother, Su Lei, had secretly asked her whether the brother who ran a company hired first-years in middle school, he wanted to earn money to buy a phone too.

    “What did you say?”

    “I said they don’t hire primary school kids,” said Su Tang. “He said he’s in first year of middle school. I said first year of middle school is still primary school. He’s furious, he’s still not speaking to me.”

    The fence was finished. The three sheep wandered round and round inside it, and one pressed its face against the fence, looking at them.

    Su Tang’s character crouched outside the fence for a moment, stood up, then crouched again. When she crouched and stood up in the game, it meant she was thinking something over; Gu Xuerong knew that by now.

    “Um…” said Su Tang. “This afternoon you said your dad owes people money. I-I’m not trying to pry, if you don’t want to say—”

    “Enzyme drink,” said Gu Xuerong.

    “…What?”

    “A kind of liquid. In bottles, yellow, they said drinking it cures illness. Lowers blood pressure, lowers blood sugar, weight loss, beauty, cures everything,” said Gu Xuerong. “He sold it with that auntie. A few years ago. First you pay out of your own pocket for stock, a big batch, then sell it to other people, and they buy stock and sell it on further down. The more you sell, the more money the people above give you.”

    “Isn’t that…”

    “Mm.”

    A sheep baa-ed inside the fence.

    “At first it sold. To relatives, to the people on the building sites, to the parents of Tiantian’s kindergarten classmates. Then it stopped selling. It piled up at home, most of all in the kitchen, case after case, from the floor up to the roof beam. My bed was in between the cases,” said Gu Xuerong. “At night when I slept, I could smell it, sour, a bit like vinegar gone off.”

    Su Tang’s character stopped crouching, and stood still.

    “Then it went out of date,” said Gu Xuerong. “He had me take it to the ditch behind the house and pour it away. Unscrew bottle after bottle and pour. It took a week. For more than a month afterwards that ditch smelled of it, and the neighbours came round to curse.”

    “…How much money did you pour away?”

    “Don’t know. He borrowed money to buy the stock. He’s still paying it back.”

    She set the last fence post, closing a gap.

    “He owed money before too,” she said. “Grandma said. Grandma said when he was young he got in a fight and stabbed someone with a knife, didn’t kill him, but paid them a lot of money, sold the house even. Grandma said that was when my mum saw him for what he was.”

    “Your grandma told you that?”

    “Not told me. Said it at the table,” said Gu Xuerong. “They talked whether I was there or not. My uncle’s wife said things too. She said later he took a fancy to a woman who ran a hair salon, bought her gold necklaces, paid her son’s school fees, chased her for two years, and she married someone else. She said whatever he’d saved those years, he threw all that in too.”

    She said it very flatly, like reading out accounts, item by item, no lead-in at the front, no summing up at the end.

    “This auntie now,” she said, “is the third.”

    Su Tang’s character stood where it was for a good while.

    Gu Xuerong thought she had frozen.

    Then Su Tang said: “Xuerong, a sheep’s got out.”

    “What?”

    “On your side, that corner, there’s a gap.” Su Tang’s voice was suddenly urgent. “One’s got out! It’s heading for the river! Quick quick quick—”

    Gu Xuerong turned round, and sure enough, a sheep was ambling out of the corner of the fence, next to the gap she had just filled— she had filled the wrong block— and walked down to the river and lowered its head to eat grass.

    The two of them gave chase.

    The sheep wouldn’t come; a rope wouldn’t hold it. Su Tang said lure it with wheat, Gu Xuerong had no wheat, Su Tang said then go and cut grass, grass drops seeds, no, seeds won’t do, it has to be wheat, Gu Xuerong said then what do we do, Su Tang said then push it, and the two of them pushed the sheep, one behind the other, one push and it moved one block, one push and it moved one block. Halfway there, Su Tang accidentally pushed it into the river, and the sheep floated in the water baa-ing, and Su Tang laughed on voice chat until she could hardly breathe, saying sorry sorry sorry, I didn’t mean to, this poor sheep.

    In the end it was Gu Xuerong who went into the water and shoved it back up, block by block, from behind.

    By the time the sheep was back in the pen, it was nearly one.

    “I should sleep,” said Gu Xuerong.

    “Mm! Then go to sleep!” said Su Tang. “Tomorrow I start work, my first day as customer service, I’m so nervous.”

    “You’re not nervous.”

    “I am nervous!”

    “You can talk to anyone.”

    “That’s because…” Su Tang got halfway and didn’t finish. “Never mind, go to sleep, good night!”

    6. Three Times

    The walls of Lin Xiaoman’s house were brick, unplastered, and didn’t keep sound in.

    After midnight she was still bent over the little table by her bed copying out biology. The desk lamp was one she had bought in middle school; its shade had a crack in it, stuck together with clear tape, and a strip of light leaked through the crack and fell slanting across the wall. Chapter two was done, and in chapter three she was on the fourth key point, three times each. When her hand ached she shook it, and carried on copying.

    In the next room, her dad was on the phone.

    “…they say the start of next month. The factory’s laying on coaches, door to door, straight from the county to the factory gate, no stopping on the way.” Her dad’s voice came through the wall, muffled. “You need a health certificate, the village issues it, the county stamps it… yeah, yeah, I know. Places? They say it goes by coach, first come first served…”

    The call ended.

    Her mum asked: “Is there still enough money?”

    “Enough till March.”

    “And Xiaoman’s living money for next term?”

    “Borrow it for now. Once we’re at the factory, we’ll pay it back out of the first month’s wages.”

    “Borrow from who?”

    “…We’ll see.”

    Lin Xiaoman’s pen stopped on the line “The main components of the cell membrane are lipids and proteins,” stopped on the last stroke of “proteins.”

    She finished the stroke, and went on copying.

    The main components of the cell membrane are lipids and proteins.

    The main components of the cell membrane are lipids and proteins.

    When she had copied it the third time, she picked up her phone.

    xuerong are you asleep

    Two minutes later, a reply.

    about to
    i got one of chen xis three variations right!!!
    which one
    the first one
    the first one was only one number different from the original
    thats still right

    Lin Xiaoman sent a sticker, a rabbit spinning round on the spot.

    have you copied out your biology
    no
    you have to copy it three times
    mm
    ill take a picture when ive finished tomorrow you can copy from it its quicker
    you copy yours
    i can get through it! im fast
    your hand aches
    …how do you know
    this afternoon you shook your hand it whooshed on the call

    Lin Xiaoman looked at this line and laughed out loud, then quickly clapped her hand over her mouth in case next door heard.

    then ill copy a bit less tomorrow and send you half
    ok
    good night!!
    good night

    She turned her phone face down on the table and pushed the lamp further in, so the strip of light leaking from the crack wouldn’t fall on the door. Chapter three, fifth key point. She copied it the first time.

    7. v0.1

    The first version came out twelve days later.

    Rice Cake had been drawn by the girl from the shop’s street promoters who could draw, copied from the cat in the video, and it was a very good likeness, the face especially, the eyes wide and round, as if the whole world owed it a cat treat. The background was the cat café windowsill, and outside the windowsill was Back Street, with the braised-meat stall’s sign on it, the characters on the sign blurred, impossible to read.

    Big Liu sent the test build to a newly made group, with three people in it: Big Liu, Ye Zhixing, Hibernation.

    When Big Liu woke at seven the next morning, there was a document in the group, sent at twelve fifty-eight in the morning.

    Rice Cake’s Diet v0.1 Test Notes　Hibernation

    1. After eating three, if you tap pause and resume quickly over and over, treats that fall during the pause get counted, and the count goes negative. Once it’s negative Rice Cake can eat forever and doesn’t get fat. I ate four hundred and something. Rice Cake didn’t get bigger, but the eating sound kept playing, stacked on top of itself, like rain. No crash.

    2. If you keep walking left, you can walk off the screen. Outside is black, no floor, Rice Cake doesn’t fall, and treats don’t fall there either. I walked left for forty minutes. There’s nothing. No edge. Suggest adding a wall. Or putting something there.

    3. If you switch to the background halfway through a rewarded video and switch back, you revive straight away, the ad didn’t finish playing. Big Liu, you’ll lose money.

    4. First place on the leaderboard is me, 413 treats. Because of item 1. Please delete it.

    5. Rice Cake meows when it wants a treat. The real Rice Cake doesn’t meow. The real Rice Cake sits, two paws together, tail covering them, looking at you.

    That’s all. Before one in the morning. Didn’t go over time.

    Big Liu read the document from top to bottom and sent a voice message to the group. In it his baby was crying, and he was talking under his breath.

    “Boss Ye, where did you find this person?”

    Ye Zhixing replied:

    number seven on the whole server

    Big Liu sent another voice message.

    “I just tried number three, it really works. Number one works too. Number two,” at his end the baby cried louder, he hushed it a couple of times, “number two, I’ll go and add a wall. Number five… OK, I’ll take the meow out, change it to sitting. The tail over the paws, I’ll get the artist to draw another frame.”

    A while later, Hibernation typed a line in the group.

    what colour should the wall be

    Big Liu replied:

    you choose
    white
    ok
    Chapter Sixteen

    Flexible

    4,994 words · about 22 min

    1. Interviews

    The first interviewee’s cat got into the shot.

    It was a tabby, which emerged from the bottom left of the frame and walked across the keyboard, leaving a long string of “ggggggggggggg” in the code editor on screen. The man on the other end was twenty-eight or twenty-nine, from Hangzhou, had worked three years at a company making HTML5 mini-games, and had a very good CV. He lifted the cat down, said sorry about that, and then said: “Mr. Ye, I’ll be straight with you. Remote is fine, twenty-two thousand a month, with social insurance and housing fund paid on the Hangzhou base. If you don’t pay those, twenty-five thousand.”

    Ye Zhixing wrote the figure down on paper, and when he’d written it, drew a circle round it.

    “We’re in a county town here.”

    “I know,” said the man. “That’s why I’m asking that much. Can you find anyone who knows Cocos where you are?”

    They couldn’t. Everyone knew that.

    The second was from Zhengzhou, and his price was reasonable, twelve thousand. Big Liu asked him three questions. He answered the first well, stumbled over the second, and for the third said “one moment, let me think,” after which there came from the call a very faint sound of typing, and that rustle of a Baidu results page being scrolled. Big Liu muted his own microphone and sent Ye Zhixing a WeChat message: he’s searching.

    Ye Zhixing replied: I can hear.

    The third was a local, twenty years old, who had done half a year of front-end at a training school in the city and sent a photo of his completion certificate, gold characters on red. Ye Zhixing had him share his screen and write a button: click once, the number goes up by one. He wrote for twenty minutes, and got it done; click once, and the number went up by two.

    “…Is that a bug?” he asked.

    “What do you think?” said Big Liu.

    “I’ll go and have another look.”

    The fourth didn’t show; half an hour after the agreed time, a message came saying the internet at home was down. The fifth showed up, and the first thing he asked was “Is your company listed?”

    Nine interviews in one week.

    On Friday evening, Ye Zhixing sat at the bar counter upstairs at the cat café, wrote the nine names on a sheet of paper, and crossed them out one by one. When he got to the last one, the pen ran dry; he switched to a red one and finished the line.

    Big Liu was on the video call holding his baby, who had just finished his milk and was hiccuping with his head on his father’s shoulder.

    “Boss Ye, maybe just go with the Hangzhou guy,” he said. “He’s expensive, but he can really do the work.”

    “Twenty-five thousand a month,” said Ye Zhixing, “and the mini-game hasn’t made a cent yet.”

    “Then the Zhengzhou one. So he searches, who doesn’t search when they code.”

    “He searched in the interview.”

    “…Fair enough.”

    The baby let out a very loud hiccup, and Big Liu patted his back and said “good boy.”

    “Actually, the few of us we’ve got now,” said Big Liu, “it’s not like we can’t do it. We’re just slow. I’m writing the game on my own and keeping an eye on the Town Matters back end too, Xiaowen’s training Su Tang, the two street promoters can’t go out right now, so they’re at home drawing and recording sound effects. If we’re really going to run several lines at once, there aren’t enough of us.”

    “I know.”

    “So what kind of person are you looking for?”

    Ye Zhixing thought about it.

    “Cheap, no good now, good in a year.”

    Big Liu laughed, so hard the baby on his shoulder bounced. “Then you’re not looking for an employee, you’re looking for an apprentice.”

    “More or less.”

    “Apprentices are hard to find,” said Big Liu. “The ones who can learn don’t need a job, and the ones who need a job can’t necessarily learn.”

    Ye Zhixing turned the sheet of crossed-out names over and wrote one word on the back: wait. Having written it, he found it funny himself, scrunched the paper up and threw it into the cardboard box of cat-litter bags under the bar.

    That evening, he sent Gu Xuerong a message.

    testing doesnt have to be on a schedule any more
    when theres a new build big liu will post it in the group test whenever you like
    just get me the report within two days

    A few minutes later, she replied.

    flexible?
    mm
    then ill test at three
    uncle he said not past three
    uncle hes not in the group
    hell ask me i dont want to lie to him

    The other end went quiet. Ye Zhixing thought she wasn’t going to reply, and got up to top up Your Highness’s water. When he came back, there was one more message on the phone:

    two
    one
    one thirty
    …fine
    deal

    Ye Zhixing looked at the word “deal” and couldn’t help smiling. Who did she learn that from, he thought. Chen Xi, probably.

    2. Snow

    In mid-March it snowed again.

    Not much; the fine, scattered kind, snowing all night, so that in the morning there was a thin layer on the ground, and where cars passed it turned to black water. There was nobody on Back Street. The braised-meat stall’s tin cart was covered with a blue tarpaulin, snow lying on the tarp, its four corners weighed down with bricks. On the copy shop’s roller shutter there was a sheet of A4, printed: Closed during the epidemic, phone in case of urgent matters. Under the phone number, someone had added a line in biro: what counts as urgent.

    The internet café’s door was shut, and the plastic strip curtain at the entrance had frozen stiff; when the wind blew, the strips knocked against each other, clack, clack.

    In the epidemic section of Town Matters, requests for supplies were fewer every day. At the start of the month it had been forty or fifty a day; now it was ten or so, mostly asking about medicine, asking when they could go out, asking how to hand in the kids’ homework. Rice, noodles and oil had basically all been delivered, and vegetables were getting through. The supermarkets had opened, and every two days each household could send one person out, with the pass from the neighbourhood committee, for two hours at most.

    The last batch of supplies for the estate where Ye Zhixing volunteered went out on Wednesday. The woman from the neighbourhood committee gave every volunteer a certificate of merit, printed on A4, with a red stamp on it and the names handwritten; on his, the “zhi” in Ye Zhixing had been written as a different “zhi,” the one that means “wise.”

    He took a photo of the certificate and posted it in the group.

    ye wise-xing hahahahahahaha
    Chen Xi: wise is good, classier than your real name
    Lin Xiaoman: i want a certificate!! our village didnt give out certificates
    Su Tang: comrade ye wise-xing!! thank you for your service!!
    Ye Zhixia: i’ve already stuck it up over the litter box

    On Chen Xi’s side, business was a little too good.

    The online classes had stopped, the homework had been handed out, and nobody could do it. Forty-odd people in a class, forty-odd people facing the same set of papers, and the last long question, no more than three people in the whole class could do it, and one of them was Chen Xi.

    His QQ group classes went from one a day to three a day: maths in the morning, physics in the afternoon, questions in the evening. Questions were charged per problem, five yuan each. It wasn’t only Class Seven coming any more; there were people from Class Eight, Class Three, and two from Year Two who got someone to bring them into the group, and the first thing they said was “hello, senior,” and Chen Xi said I’m Year One, and the guy said hello, junior then, and Chen Xi said that’s not right either, call me Mr. Chen.

    “Ten yuan a lesson,” Lin Xiaoman worked it out for him in the group, “forty people a lesson, four hundred. Three lessons a day, twelve hundred. Plus the questions.”

    “Not that much,” said Chen Xi. “Some people come in and don’t pay.”

    “So what do you do?”

    “Kick them.”

    “…That’s still several hundred a day.”

    “Mm.”

    “Chen Xi, you’re rich.” Lin Xiaoman sent a kowtowing emoji. “Tens of thousands a month.”

    “Not that much,” said Chen Xi. “It stops when school starts.”

    “Why stop?”

    “Once school starts, who’s going to pay to hear me explain things.”

    That was true. But what he didn’t say was something else. Last Wednesday, the physics teacher had posted in the class group, “A number of students have said the homework is quite hard; I can use my spare time to give one-to-one tutoring to students who need it, message me privately for details.” Less than an hour after it went up, the message was withdrawn. The next day, Zheng Xin forwarded a document from the county education bureau to the group, with a very long title, the gist of which was that serving teachers were strictly forbidden from giving paid tutoring in any form, online or offline, and that anyone found doing so would be dealt with severely.

    The physics teacher never posted in the group again.

    Chen Xi saw the “message withdrawn” notice, saw the document, said nothing, and that evening added another class.

    He wasn’t a teacher. The document didn’t apply to him.

    Lin Xiaoman was still copying.

    Biology finished, she was copying chemical equations, five times each this time, a rule she’d made herself. She had filled one physics mistakes notebook and started another. Of the three variations Chen Xi set, she could now get two right; the third she still couldn’t, the third always came at it from some angle she had never seen.

    “Stop memorizing,” Chen Xi said on the call. “Think about it: who’s giving this force to whom.”

    “I did think.”

    “And what did you get?”

    “…I couldn’t work it out, so I memorized it.”

    Chen Xi went quiet. On the call there was only the sound of his chopsticks tapping a bowl, ting, ting, ting, three times.

    “Then write down the places where you can’t work it out,” he said. “Every time you can’t work it out, write one line: which step you got stuck on. When you’ve filled a page, take a photo and send it to me.”

    “Do I have to pay for that?”

    “No.”

    “No discounts for classmates.”

    “This isn’t a class,” said Chen Xi. “This is me wanting to know where you get stuck.”

    Lin Xiaoman’s end was quiet for a moment, then came the sound of pages turning.

    “OK,” she said. “Then I’ll write it.”

    3. The Phone Call

    The call came to the cat café’s landline.

    The cat café’s landline number was on the opening-hours sign at the door, and on the shop’s page on Town Matters; normally it didn’t ring twice a month, and when it did it was mostly people asking whether Rice Cake was still there, or whether they could bring their own cat to play. Since the lockdown it hadn’t rung at all.

    A little after three that afternoon, it rang. Ye Zhixia was lying across the bar counter doing maths, closest to it, and reached out and answered.

    “Hello, Back Street Cats—”

    “Where’s your boss?” A woman’s voice, very sharp. “Put your boss on.”

    Ye Zhixia looked at her brother and covered the mouthpiece. “It’s for you. Some auntie, really fierce.”

    Ye Zhixing took it.

    “Speaking.”

    “You’re the one called Ye?” said the woman. “Gu Xuerong works for you, right? I’m her mum.”

    Ye Zhixing didn’t correct her.

    “What can I do for you?”

    “Plenty,” said the woman. “She’s a child, working for you, how much are you paying her? Where’s the money? Is it all going to her? She’s a minor, what does she know about money. We’re her guardians, the money should come to us. We’ll keep it safe for her.”

    “Her wages,” said Ye Zhixing, “by the regulations can only be paid to her.”

    “What regulations?”

    “Article Six of the Interim Provisions on Wage Payment,” said Ye Zhixing. Uncle He had told him this a couple of days earlier; he had asked Uncle He to send him the original text and read it twice. “The employer shall pay wages to the worker in person.”

    There was a moment’s silence at the other end.

    “…And if she can’t collect it?” The woman’s voice changed key. “Don’t the regulations also say that if the person can’t collect it themselves, a relative can collect it for them? I’m her relative.”

    Ye Zhixing was a little surprised. She actually knew that clause.

    “She can collect it herself,” he said. “And she hasn’t authorized you.”

    “She’s a child, what does she know about authorizing—”

    “Auntie,” said Ye Zhixing, “she’s sixteen.”

    Another voice came down the line, a man’s, some way from the receiver, slurred, too indistinct to make out, but Ye Zhixing had heard that tone before, at the door of that single-storey house in the urban village. The woman said something to the man, then came back to the phone.

    “Right, so you won’t pay up,” she said. “I’m telling you, once the lockdown’s over, we’ll come to that shop of yours—”

    “You’re welcome,” said Ye Zhixing. “Book ahead before you come. Shop rules: customers can’t pick up the cats without asking.”

    He hung up.

    Ye Zhixia was still lying across the bar counter, her pen not moving.

    “Bro,” she said, “that was Sister Xuerong’s stepmum?”

    “Yeah.”

    “Will she call again?”

    “She will.”

    She did call again. Three times the next day, five times the day after. On the third evening it was a different number, the man, who started cursing the moment the call connected and cursed for a full minute and more; Ye Zhixing put the receiver down on the bar counter, went to change the cats’ water bowl, and when he came back the other end was still cursing. He picked it up and said: “Finished? If you’re finished I’m hanging up.”

    Afterwards he blocked both numbers.

    The landline couldn’t block numbers, so he unplugged it.

    Ye Zhixia asked: “Should we tell Sister Xuerong?”

    Ye Zhixing thought for a moment. “She knows.”

    “How do you know she knows?”

    “They called her first,” said Ye Zhixing. “When they couldn’t get through, they called here.”

    4. Brushing

    Your Highness hadn’t been outside all winter, and its fur had grown like a scarf trailing on the floor.

    A Ragdoll’s coat is long, a layer of down underneath and a layer of long hair on top; if you don’t brush it, it knots, and once a knot is tight, the only thing to do is cut it. Ye Zhixia dug two combs out of the storeroom: a slicker brush with bent wire teeth, and a steel comb, half wide teeth, half fine. She handed the slicker to her brother and kept the comb.

    “Use that first to loosen the undercoat,” she said, “then I’ll go through from the head with this. Be gentle, Your Highness doesn’t like pain.”

    “Doesn’t like pain?” said Ye Zhixing. “It drew blood on the Devon yesterday.”

    “The Devon started it.”

    Your Highness lay on Ye Zhixing’s lap belly up, four paws in the air, eyes half closed, an air of do what you like. Ye Zhixing drew the brush through once and pulled out a clump of grey-white down, light as anything, which the electric heater’s breeze lifted and stuck in Ye Zhixia’s hair.

    Rice Cake was waiting beside them. It wasn’t long-haired and didn’t need brushing, but when it saw Your Highness being brushed it had to come and squeeze in, squeezing into Ye Zhixia’s lap, butting her hand with its head, butt, butt. Ye Zhixia had no choice but to give it a couple of strokes with the comb too, and when she’d done it lay down, satisfied, and spread its belly out.

    Calico appeared from somewhere, jumped onto the back of the sofa, and rubbed against the back of Ye Zhixing’s head from behind.

    “They think you’re a cat tree,” said Ye Zhixia.

    “I am one.”

    Outside it was nearly dark. The snow on the roof opposite hadn’t melted, a white layer with a black rim round the edge, which was the tiles.

    Brushing Rice Cake, Ye Zhixia asked as she brushed: “Bro, do you like Sister Xuerong?”

    Ye Zhixing’s hands didn’t stop.

    “Where did you hear that.”

    “I didn’t hear it anywhere, I worked it out,” said Ye Zhixia. “You took her a fridge, you found her a job, her stepmum calls and you have a row with her—”

    “I didn’t have a row.”

    “You hung up on her.”

    “That’s not a row, that’s ending a call.”

    Ye Zhixia rolled her eyes. Rice Cake rolled over on her lap and switched to the other side of its belly.

    “Between people,” said Ye Zhixing, “it’s not only like or don’t like.”

    “Then what is it?”

    He picked the clump of down off the slicker, rolled it into a little ball, and squeezed it in his hand.

    “When I see her,” he said, “I think of some things from before.”

    “That thing three years ago?”

    Ye Zhixing didn’t take that up. He put the ball of fluff on Your Highness’s belly; Your Highness looked at it and didn’t move.

    “Zhixia,” he said, “someone like me, you tell me, do I really have the right to save anyone?”

    The comb in Ye Zhixia’s hand stopped.

    “…What are you on about,” she said. She bent her head to brush Rice Cake, brushing very hard, and Rice Cake meowed and turned to glare at her. She brushed more gently. “What are you on about. You’ll always be the best brother.”

    “That’s a different thing.”

    “It’s not a different thing,” said Ye Zhixia. “You just are.”

    Ye Zhixing didn’t argue with her.

    Your Highness’s belly was done, and he turned it over to do its back. Your Highness wasn’t keen, wriggled a couple of times, and in the end lay down, its tail slapping his thigh, again and again.

    “So now you’re out, what are you going to do?” Ye Zhixia asked. “Just live at the shop?”

    “Local stuff first,” said Ye Zhixing. “Town Matters, the mini-games, the company’s other lines, hold up what can be held up. In a couple of years, go to a big city.”

    “Which big city?”

    “Haven’t decided. Wherever there are the most chances.”

    “And me?”

    “You go to school.”

    “I mean,” said Ye Zhixia, “what can I help with?”

    Ye Zhixing glanced at her. There was still Your Highness’s fur stuck in her hair, wisp after wisp, grey-white; she didn’t know.

    “You don’t have to help with anything,” he said. “You just be fine, eat, play, get into high school. Leave the rest to me. It’s fine.”

    “There you go again.”

    “What?”

    “You said that last time too,” said Ye Zhixia. “Three years ago, you said it was fine too. And then you stood outside on your own all night.”

    The slicker in Ye Zhixing’s hand stopped on Your Highness’s back.

    “…Mum and Dad don’t really like me much either,” said Ye Zhixia. She said it very fast, as if trying to finish before she regretted it. “Dad only cares whether you’re useful, and when you’re not, he yells at you. I’ve never been useful, so he can’t even be bothered to yell at me. Mum just cries, and when she’s done crying she does whatever Dad says. In that house you’re the only one who’s good to me.”

    “So?”

    “So stop carrying everything on your own,” she said. “I’m fourteen, I can cook, I can do accounts, I can clip cats’ claws. I can help mind the shop, I can help answer Town Matters messages. Can Sister Su Tang keep up on her own? She’s answering till midnight.”

    Ye Zhixing looked at her.

    After a good while, he reached out and picked the wisp of cat fur out of her hair, picked one wisp, and there was another, and picked again.

    “Your hair’s full of Your Highness,” he said.

    “…Don’t change the subject.”

    “Town Matters,” he said, “I’ll ask Xiaowen tomorrow which part she can hand over to you. Not the help requests, the ones asking about opening hours. An hour a day, after your homework.”

    Ye Zhixia’s eyes lit up.

    “Is it paid?”

    “No,” said Ye Zhixing. “You’re not sixteen, you can’t sign.”

    “So I work for nothing?”

    “You eat my food and live under my roof.”

    “That’s what you’re supposed to do.”

    “Then count it as your board.”

    Ye Zhixia thought about it, decided she didn’t seem to be losing out, and said nothing more, bending her head to go on brushing Rice Cake. Rice Cake was already asleep, purring very softly.

    5. Blocks

    A little after midnight that night, when Su Tang found Gu Xuerong in MC, she was sitting on the roof of the little wooden house.

    The roof was pitched, and she sat on the ridge with her two legs—block legs—dangling over one side. In the sky was a square moon, and square clouds drifting slowly in one direction, block by block.

    In the forest across the river there were a few bee nests hanging from the branches, yellow, a swarm of block bees buzzing round them. They had come in with the new version last winter; the first time Su Tang saw them she shrieked, “Bees!! There are bees now!!”, ran over and poked at them, the buzzing suddenly got very loud, she shrieked again, turned and fled, and ran into the river.

    That night they had gone to collect honey. Su Tang had looked up a guide, which said to light a campfire under the nest and the smoke would stop the bees stinging, then use a glass bottle to collect it. They lit the campfire, got glass bottles, collected three bottles, and Su Tang drank all three in one go and said “sweet!”, and Gu Xuerong asked how she knew it was sweet when she drank it in a game, and Su Tang said I just know.

    When they got back, Gu Xuerong climbed onto the roof, and Su Tang climbed up too and sat down beside her.

    Two block people sitting on the ridge of a roof, looking at a square moon.

    “Xuerong.”

    “Mm.”

    “…Can I ask you some things?”

    “Ask.”

    For a long time there was no sound from Su Tang. Gu Xuerong thought she had frozen again and was about to speak when Su Tang began, her voice lower than usual, slower than usual, as if moving the words out of her mouth one at a time.

    “The braised pork day,” she said. “When you moved the pot up in front of the phone so I could see the colour. Your sleeve caught on the rim of the pot and slid up a bit.”

    Gu Xuerong’s block person didn’t move.

    “I saw,” said Su Tang. “I didn’t say anything then, I was afraid if I said something you’d turn the video off. But I kept thinking about it afterwards. For days and days.”

    “…”

    “I want to ask you,” said Su Tang, “why do you… still shut yourself in so tight? Your arm, what happened? Why would you do that? And, later on… have you got any plans?”

    She asked it all in one breath, and when she had asked it, sniffed first herself.

    Gu Xuerong didn’t answer on voice.

    After a while, a line popped up in the chat bar at the bottom left of the screen.

    <Hibernation> who knows

    Another line.

    <Hibernation> have i shut myself in

    <Hibernation> haha

    <Hibernation> i know

    <Hibernation> but i cant get out yet

    Su Tang looked at the lines and made no sound.

    The chat bar stayed still for a long time. The moon moved one block west. Across the river, the bees flew back to their nest and crawled in one by one.

    <Hibernation> why do that

    <Hibernation> maybe i thought about it too

    <Hibernation> ending all of it

    On voice, Su Tang made a small sound, very short, and clamped it back down herself.

    <Hibernation> plans i never thought about

    <Hibernation> i think there used to be things i wanted

    <Hibernation> then they all broke

    <Hibernation> once theyre broken you stop thinking about them saves trouble

    <Hibernation> dont look at the arm

    <Hibernation> its not nice to look at

    <Hibernation> just leave me be

    That last line stayed in the chat bar, and after ten seconds or so slowly faded and disappeared.

    For a long time there was no sound from Su Tang. Gu Xuerong heard a little sniffing, very suppressed, one, then another, and the rustle of a tissue being pulled from its packet.

    “…No,” said Su Tang.

    Her voice was hoarse, and thick with her nose.

    “I won’t leave you be,” she said. “You say leave me be, and I just leave you be? Then all those meals I brought were for nothing. Braised pork lessons for nothing. Honey collected for nothing.”

    “You drank the honey.”

    “I still collected it!” said Su Tang, and sniffed again. “Xuerong, I don’t know how to say it. My mum says I’m bad with words, I can’t talk properly about serious things, I just chatter. I’m no good at it. But you listen, I’m only saying it once.”

    “Mm.”

    “Whatever happens,” said Su Tang, “wherever you go later, whatever you do, whatever you turn into, we’re best friends. Forever. Let’s make a promise, OK?”

    For a good while there was nothing in the chat bar.

    <Hibernation> what if the promise breaks

    Su Tang was thrown for a moment.

    “…Then we promise again!” she said. “If it breaks, we promise again. However many times it breaks, we promise that many times.”

    <Hibernation> then it doesnt count as a promise

    “It counts!” said Su Tang. “If I say it counts, it counts!”

    The chat bar was empty again.

    The square moon was still moving west. Gu Xuerong’s block person moved on the ridge, turned its head, and looked at Su Tang beside it. A block person’s face is flat; its two eyes were two little black squares, with no expression.

    <Hibernation> ok

    <Hibernation> promise

    Su Tang let out a sob, and this time didn’t clamp it down, and cried properly. Crying, she said “wait a sec,” “I’m getting a tissue,” “we’re out of tissues,” “I’ll use my brother’s towel,” and then on the call came her brother’s sleepy voice: “Sis, why are you using my towel…”, “Go back to sleep!”

    Gu Xuerong listened from her end.

    By the time Su Tang came back, her nose was so blocked her voice came out muffled.

    “Xuerong,” she said, “your bee.”

    “What?”

    “Behind you, on the roof, there’s a bee. It followed us back.”

    Gu Xuerong turned round. There really was one, a little yellow-and-black-striped block, circling and buzzing over the roof behind her. It must have followed them over after the campfire went out.

    “Is it going to sting me?”

    “It won’t sting you. It’s just lost,” said Su Tang. “Bees go back to the nest at night, it can’t find its home.”

    Gu Xuerong looked at the bee.

    “So what do we do.”

    “Don’t know,” said Su Tang. “The guide didn’t say.”

    The bee circled a few times and landed on the roof, right beside Gu Xuerong’s block person, and stopped flying.

    Neither of them did anything about it.

    6. Beanpole

    The next morning, Chen Xi sent Ye Zhixing a private message.

    you were looking for someone to write code found anyone
    no
    beanpole can code

    Ye Zhixing had to think for a moment to remember who Beanpole was. The tallest of the lot from the internet café, skinny, his neck even longer than Chen Xi’s; that time on Back Street when they pinned Gu Jianguo down, he had held the left arm.

    what can he write
    cheats
    e language button wizard
    pubg crossfire hes written a few sold them
    then he got banned stopped writing them
    never went to school quit in the second year of middle school
    hes not stupid
    why are you telling me
    youre looking for someone he needs money
    his familys internet cafe is shut right now hes stuck at home getting yelled at by his mum every day
    just saying try him if you want if not forget it

    Ye Zhixing looked at the lines, put the phone down, and picked it up again.

    tell him to add me

    Half an hour later a new friend request popped up, the avatar a CrossFire screenshot, the name “Beanpole”, and in the reason field: brother xi told me to add you. hello brother ye.

    Ye Zhixing accepted and sent a message:

    write something in js do you know js
    no
    i can learn
    write a button click once and the number goes up by one
    send it to me when its done
    no rush
    ok

    That afternoon, while Ye Zhixing was clipping Your Highness’s claws, his phone pinged. He freed a hand to look: a file from Beanpole, followed by a line:

    i searched it learned for three hours got it done
    click once it goes up one
    i also added one if you click ten times it changes colour
    dont know if you want that if not ill delete it

    Ye Zhixing opened the file and clicked once, and the number went from 0 to 1. He clicked nine more times, and the background went from white to blue.

    He sent the screenshot to Big Liu.

    Big Liu replied with three words:

    taking an apprentice?

    Ye Zhixing replied:

    trying him out
    Chapter Seventeen

    Mediation

    7,591 words · about 33 min

    1. Huang Yingjun

    Beanpole came in mid-March, the day after the checkpoint at the estate gates was taken down.

    He stood at the foot of the stairs below the cat café, so tall that the stairwell bulb hung right in front of his forehead and he had to crook his neck. He wore a black windbreaker washed nearly grey, his mask hooked over one ear, and held an old laptop to his chest, a Lenovo, its lid covered in stickers, half of them CrossFire guns and half anime girls, the corners curling where they had worn.

    “Brother Ye.”

    “Come on up.”

    He came up, banged his head on the door frame on the way in, thunk. Rice Cake raised its head from the windowsill, looked at him, and lay back down.

    Uncle He was there that day, sitting at the bar counter with a folder and a stack of forms in front of him. Ye Zhixing said fill in the registration stuff first, and Uncle He pushed a form and a pen across.

    “Name.”

    Beanpole held the pen and didn’t write.

    “Go on.”

    “…Huang Yingjun,” he said. “As in ‘handsome.’ Go on, laugh. Everyone does.”

    Ye Zhixing didn’t laugh. Behind the bar, Ye Zhixia, crouched topping up the cat bowls, let out a “pfft” and quickly buried her face in the cat-food bag.

    “Age,” said Uncle He.

    “Sixteen. Just turned, last month.”

    “Brought your ID?”

    He took it out of the inside pocket of his windbreaker and handed it over. Uncle He took it, held it under his reading glasses for a while, checked the date of birth, nodded, and wrote it on the form.

    “Where do you live?”

    “North of town, the textile machinery factory housing. My grandma’s flat.”

    “Living with your grandma?”

    “Grandma died the year before last,” said Huang Yingjun. “I live on my own.”

    Uncle He’s pen paused. “Your parents?”

    “Divorced. Both found someone else. My dad’s in Zhengzhou, my mum’s in the city, they both have kids now.” He said it very smoothly, like a passage he had learned by heart. “They left me the flat to live in, and my mum transfers me a thousand a month. When she calls, it’s to yell at me, and when she’s done yelling she transfers the money.”

    “School?”

    “Stopped in the second year of middle school.”

    “Why?”

    “I kept not going, and the homeroom teacher said if you don’t come again, don’t bother coming,” said Huang Yingjun. “So I didn’t.”

    Uncle He put down the pen, took off his reading glasses, and wiped them on the hem of his jacket.

    “That’s not you stopping,” he said. “That’s them breaking the law. Nine years’ compulsory education; a school isn’t allowed to push anyone out.”

    Huang Yingjun stopped short, as if hearing this for the first time. “…Well, it’s too late now.”

    “Mm.” Uncle He put his glasses back on. “Now it’s too late.” He started a new line at the bottom of the form and wrote a few words. “Medical check when the hospitals open. Juvenile worker, there are jobs you can’t do: lifting heavy things, working at heights, staying up all night, none of those. Young master, the staying up all night part, you heard that.”

    “I heard,” said Ye Zhixing.

    It wasn’t that Ye Zhixing couldn’t code; it was that what he could do was the wrong kind.

    He wrote Python: scraping data, crunching numbers, a few batch scripts for the Town Matters back end, all his own work. C++ he had learned for the informatics olympiad in middle school, good enough for algorithm problems. But games needed a different set of things: JS, engines, animation, working it all out frame by frame, and he couldn’t find a way in. The pages of the very first version of Town Matters he had pieced together from online tutorials; they worked, but they were ugly, and later Big Liu rewrote all of it. He could read Big Liu’s code, change a bit, spot where the logic was wrong, but ask him to write a game from scratch and he couldn’t do it.

    So it was Big Liu who taught Huang Yingjun.

    The two of them were on video, screen-sharing, Big Liu explaining at his end and Huang Yingjun writing at this end. On the first day they did variables; Big Liu said give it any name you like and store a number in it. Huang Yingjun named it “shuzi,” number.

    “…Give it an English name.”

    “My English is bad.”

    “Pinyin’s fine too, but at least—” At Big Liu’s end the baby started crying; he turned to hush it and turned back. “At least don’t call it shuzi. You’ve got a hundred more numbers coming, are you calling them all shuzi?”

    “Then shuzi2.”

    At his end, Big Liu let out a very long sigh.

    But on the third day they hit a bug: on one level, when Rice Cake ate its third treat, the game froze for half a second. Big Liu spent the whole morning on it and couldn’t find it. Huang Yingjun watched his screen for a dozen minutes and said: “Is that check of yours running every frame?”

    Big Liu went to look. It was.

    “How did you spot that?”

    “When I used to write cheats,” said Huang Yingjun, “if you got a loop wrong, the game lagged. Lag once and you got detected, and the account was gone. I’ve had six accounts banned.”

    Big Liu looked at him on the video for several seconds.

    “Boss Ye,” he said later on WeChat, “this kid’s got it. Just have to straighten out all that pinyin first.”

    On the fourth day, Huang Yingjun got stuck on a problem. Not code: maths. Big Liu wanted him to write the treats falling faster and faster according to a formula, and he couldn’t understand the formula.

    “If you don’t get it, ask Chen Xi,” said Ye Zhixing. “He’s good at maths.”

    Huang Yingjun turned round.

    “Brother Xi?” he said. “He’s good at maths?”

    “Mm.”

    “He played CrossFire with us at the internet café for two years,” said Huang Yingjun. “His sniping is so-so.”

    “He’s second in the year,” said Ye Zhixing. “Second in the whole county in the high-school entrance exam. Maths and physics, nearly full marks.”

    Huang Yingjun’s mouth fell open and stayed open for a long time.

    That evening, he posted in the internet café gang’s group:

    did you lot know brother xi is a genius

    Abiao was quickest to reply:

    bullshit

    Chubby:

    last time he worked out the internet fees he was crazy fast i thought hed practised mental maths

    The youngest:

    ive seen his homework book all ticks i thought he copied it

    Abiao:

    copied from who

    The youngest:

    …dunno

    A while later, Abiao posted again:

    so why does he hang out with us every day

    Nobody answered.

    Chen Xi was in the group too, lurking the whole time. The next day, before his class, he posted one line:

    anyone who calls me xi the great again gets kicked

    2. Cat Hair

    Once March came, the cats started shedding.

    Actually they shed all year round; indoors, with heating and lights, cats can’t really tell the seasons, so they shed in winter and in summer too. But in spring they shed worst of all, by the handful. Ye Zhixia’s black hoodie turned grey within an hour of putting it on.

    She bought a lint roller, fifty sheets a roll, and could get through twenty sheets a day.

    “Stop wearing black,” said Ye Zhixing.

    “This is the only one I brought.”

    “Then wear mine.”

    “Yours are black too.”

    In the end she wore the cat café’s work apron, beige, where the fur didn’t show much, with a comb in the front pocket, combing wherever she went. Briquette wouldn’t let her comb it; the moment she reached out it ran. Calico let her, and after two strokes rolled onto its back. Rice Cake liked it most, and when she finished it wouldn’t leave, butting her hand with its head to make her keep going.

    Your Highness had recently learned to open doors.

    The sliding door to the back room: they used to shut it in there at night, and it would sing behind the door. Now it didn’t sing. One night Ye Zhixia got up for the toilet and saw it crouched by the door, one front paw reaching out, claws hooked into the gap between door and frame; one swipe sideways and the door slid open a crack, and it squeezed out, walked up to her feet and looked up at her, without the slightest guilt.

    “How did you get out?”

    Your Highness yowled once.

    The next day she put a strip of tape on the door. The day after, the tape had been clawed off, rolled into a ball, and left beside the litter box.

    Rice Cake stole food.

    The cupboard in the storeroom where the freeze-dried treats were kept had a magnetic door that opened with a push. At first Rice Cake only knew how to sit in front of the cupboard, sitting all afternoon. Then one day Ye Zhixia came back to find the cupboard open, a bag of freeze-dried chicken bitten open and spilled all over the floor, and Rice Cake lying in the middle of the heap, its belly round as a drum. When it saw her come in it didn’t run, just burped.

    “You’re on a diet!”

    Rice Cake burped again.

    Half a tin of cat food left over, put on the bar counter under a plastic lid to feed them in the evening: in the moment it took to turn round, the lid had been pushed onto the floor, the tin was empty, and Calico was crouched on the bar licking its lips.

    Ye Zhixia wrote all of this down, item by item, on a sheet of paper stuck to the fridge door, headed “Criminal Record.” Rice Cake’s column was the longest.

    There was one more thing she couldn’t work out.

    Every time she came back from outside, changed her shoes and sat down on the sofa, the Devon would come over and sniff her socks, sniffing very carefully, from toe to ankle, then lift its head, mouth half open, lip curled up showing two little teeth, and freeze there, as if something had disgusted it, or as if it were contemplating life.

    “What does that mean?” she asked her brother. “It thinks my feet stink?”

    “It’s smelling,” said Ye Zhixing. “When cats smell certain things, they open their mouths and let the smell into that bit at the roof of the mouth, to smell it again.”

    “So it thinks my feet stink.”

    “Not necessarily. They only do it for smells they’re interested in.”

    “So it thinks my feet stink in a really interesting way.”

    Ye Zhixing thought about it, and didn’t argue.

    Rice Cake didn’t sniff socks. Rice Cake liked to rub. It pressed its cheek against her calf and rubbed from one end to the other, then switched to the other cheek and rubbed back, and when it was done, with its tail straight up, it went once round her and started rubbing again.

    “It’s stamping you,” said Ye Zhixing.

    “Stamping what?”

    “Its face has a smell; rub a bit, and you smell of it,” he said. “It doesn’t like that you went out and came back not smelling of it.”

    Ye Zhixia looked down at Rice Cake. Rice Cake rubbed once more.

    “So it does that to you too.”

    “Mm.”

    “So we both belong to it.”

    “More or less.”

    3. The Neighbourhood Committee

    That morning, they had been meant to go to the bank.

    Uncle He had booked it: the rural commercial bank in the old town, Wednesday morning, bring her ID, her labour contract, the company’s proof of income, the last few months’ wage records. Uncle He said that over sixteen, with all that, the bank would let her open an account herself, no guardian needed. But on Tuesday evening Ye Zhixing got a call from the hotpot chain in the city, the one whose ordering system had been put on hold last year: the owner said the branches were reopening next week, he wanted to carry on with the project, could they talk in person tomorrow.

    Uncle He had to drive him.

    “I’ll go with her,” Chen Xi said in the group. “Give me the stuff.”

    So Uncle He gave Chen Xi the folder. A blue plastic folder with a snap fastener, every sheet inside stacked in order, and on top a sticky note in Uncle He’s handwriting: She brings the original ID herself, copy on page one, contract page two, proof of income page three, give the teller whatever she asks for, don’t talk too much.

    Chen Xi peeled off the sticky note, read it through, and stuck it back on.

    At half past nine they met at the end of Back Street. Gu Xuerong was wearing that navy down jacket, zipped up to her chin, no hat, the little tuft at the back of her head tied a bit higher than usual. Chen Xi had the folder tucked under his arm, his cap crooked.

    “Let’s go.”

    “Mm.”

    Back Street had a little more life in it than last month. The braised-meat stall wasn’t out yet, but the copy shop’s roller shutter was half up, and the owner was sweeping inside, sweeping out a pile of dust. The internet café’s curtain was still hanging, with a sheet of paper on the door: Closed until further notice. Underneath, someone had written in marker: “please open soon begging you,” and someone else had added below: “+1”.

    “Beanpole wrote that,” said Chen Xi.

    “How do you know?”

    “He never dots the i in ‘begging.’”

    They had just come out of Back Street and turned onto the main road when Gu Xuerong’s phone rang.

    An unknown number, local. She looked at it and didn’t answer. When it stopped, it rang again, a second time. She answered.

    “Hello.”

    “Hello, is that Gu Xuerong?” A man’s voice, in his forties, very even. “This is Chengguan police station, my name’s Wang. Your father has reported that you ran away from home over two months ago and can’t be contacted. Where are you right now?”

    The other end waited a few seconds.

    “Hello? Gu Xuerong?”

    “On the street.”

    “Are you on your own?”

    “No.”

    “Here’s the thing,” said Officer Wang. “The community has you registered as living over on Back Street, such-and-such road, such-and-such number, I’ve got it here. Your parents are at the neighbourhood committee now, the one just out of Back Street, Minzhu Road community. Come over and we’ll sort it out face to face. Your parents don’t know where you live; I haven’t told them. Come over yourself.”

    The call ended.

    Gu Xuerong stood at the roadside holding her phone. An electric three-wheeler drove past her with a few sacks of cement in its bed, raising a little dust.

    “Who?” Chen Xi asked.

    “The police,” said Gu Xuerong. “They called the police.”

    Chen Xi looked at her.

    “Going?”

    “…If I don’t,” said Gu Xuerong, “they’ll come again.”

    “Mm.”

    “Then let’s go.”

    The Minzhu Road neighbourhood committee was on the ground floor of a small three-storey building, with a red banner over the door, “United as one, fight the epidemic,” and under the banner a table with a thermometer gun, a bottle of hand sanitizer and a register. A woman in a red armband stood at the door, took their temperatures, 36.2, 36.4, and had them write their names in the book.

    There were six people inside.

    Officer Wang sat by the window, about fifty, a black padded vest over his uniform, a thermos cup in front of him. Beside him stood an auxiliary officer in his early twenties, looking at his phone. The sub-district office had sent a woman in her thirties, glasses, short hair, a notebook in her hand. The community grid worker, a plump middle-aged man, sat by the door.

    Gu Jianguo and the woman sat on a long sofa.

    The moment the woman saw Gu Xuerong come in, she stood up, and her eyes went red at once.

    “Xuerong—” She took two steps forward. “You’ve finally turned up, do you know how frantic your dad and I have been looking for you? Over two months, you don’t answer calls, you don’t answer messages, over New Year, with the epidemic this bad, we haven’t slept a wink—”

    She reached out to take Gu Xuerong’s arm.

    Gu Xuerong stepped to one side. Chen Xi moved half a step in front of her.

    The woman’s hand stopped in mid-air, drew back, and wiped her eyes.

    “Who’s this?” Gu Jianguo spoke. He didn’t get up; he leaned back on the sofa, both hands on his knees, black under his fingernails. “You again.”

    “Classmate,” said Chen Xi. “The one who held you down on the street last time.”

    Gu Jianguo’s face twitched.

    “What’s a classmate tagging along for?”

    “Keeping her company while she does something.”

    “Does what?”

    “Opens a bank account.”

    Gu Jianguo’s eyes moved.

    “Sit, sit,” said Officer Wang. “Everyone sit down and talk.”

    For the next half hour, it was mostly the woman talking.

    She said the child had been rebellious since she was small, wouldn’t be told, couldn’t stand being at home, looked down on the family for being poor, for not being well off. She said the minute the holidays came she was off out, and she and the girl’s dad had tried every way of talking to her, and she just wouldn’t listen. She said over New Year her dad stood at the door every day waiting, till midnight. She said with the epidemic this bad, a sixteen-year-old girl out there on her own, what was she eating and drinking, where was she living, if anything happened what would they say to her dead—“to her real mum,” she corrected herself.

    By the end, she was crying again.

    “It’s not like we want anything,” she said. “We just want the child to come home. We’re family, what can’t be said at home? We heard she’s working out there too, minding a shop for someone, a sixteen-year-old, what does she know, whatever they give her she takes, she wouldn’t even know if she was being cheated. That money, us as her parents, keeping it safe for her, what’s wrong with that?”

    The woman from the sub-district office was taking notes, writing a few words, glancing up.

    Officer Wang picked up his thermos cup and took a sip. “Gu Xuerong,” he said, “you tell us.”

    Gu Xuerong stood there. She hadn’t sat down; there was an empty chair, and Chen Xi told her to sit, and she didn’t.

    “Why don’t you go home?”

    “…”

    “What your parents have said, is that how it is?”

    Gu Xuerong looked at Gu Jianguo.

    “Where would I sleep if I went back?” she said.

    No one in the room answered.

    “The bed in the kitchen,” she said, “is it still there.”

    Gu Jianguo’s face darkened at once.

    “You’ve got a nerve!” He stood up off the sofa. “I feed you, I clothe you, and you turn your nose up at the kitchen? Your sister’s room is your sister’s, who do you think you are—”

    “Gu Jianguo.” Officer Wang put down his cup. “Sit down.”

    “Officer, you hear this, you hear what she’s saying—”

    “Sit down.”

    Gu Jianguo sat down. The woman beside him tugged at his sleeve, twice.

    Chen Xi took out his phone, dialled a number, and put it on speaker.

    It rang four times, then connected. It was very noisy at the other end, bowls and pans clattering, someone shouting “table three.”

    “Hello.”

    “At the police—at the neighbourhood committee,” said Chen Xi. “Her dad called the police, said she ran away from home. The police are here, the sub-district office is here.”

    The other end was quiet for two seconds.

    “I’m the person responsible at her employer.” Ye Zhixing’s voice came out of the speaker. “Hello, Officer. She’s currently working at my company doing remote software testing. She has a signed labour contract and proof of income, and her wages are paid monthly. Chen Xi has the contract.”

    Chen Xi took the folder from under his arm, popped the snap, opened it, took out pages two and three, and put them on the table in front of Officer Wang.

    Officer Wang took his reading glasses out of his vest pocket, put them on, and picked them up to read.

    A labour contract: Party A a company, Party B Gu Xuerong, position software tester, remote, monthly salary two thousand five hundred. Signature, fingerprint, company seal, date.

    Proof of income, the same company seal.

    Further back, a few printed transfer records, one payment a month, the earliest last autumn.

    The woman from the sub-district office leaned over to look.

    “Article Eighteen of the General Provisions of the Civil Law,” said Ye Zhixing on the phone. “A minor aged sixteen or over whose main source of living is income from their own labour is deemed to have full capacity for civil conduct. What she eats, where she lives, rent, water and electricity, she earns all of it herself.”

    “Hear that?” said Chen Xi. “She earns her own money and spends her own money. No need for you to keep it safe for her.”

    “She’s fooling them!” said the woman. “She’s a child, what can she do, they give her money because they feel sorry for her—”

    “She hands in seven or eight test reports a month,” said Ye Zhixing on the phone. “If you hired someone outside, one report alone would cost more than that.”

    Chen Xi glanced at the phone screen. Ye Zhixing said nothing further.

    Officer Wang put the contract down and took off his glasses.

    “Right,” he said. “We understand the situation now. The child has a job, has an income, has somewhere to live, none of that’s a problem. But you’re a family, after all; it’s no good falling out like this.”

    The woman from the sub-district office took over: “Yes, the law is the law, and family is family. When a child and her family have a disagreement, you can sit down and talk it through. We have a mediation room at the sub-district office, with a proper mediator, why don’t we all go to the mediation room and clear the air?”

    “Sounds good to me,” said Officer Wang. “And, er… the person on the phone, Mr. Ye, is it? As the person responsible at her employer, it would be best if you came over too.”

    “I can’t make it,” said Ye Zhixing.

    “Hm?”

    “I’m in the city in meetings, my whole day is booked,” he said. “We’re a micro business, seven or eight people in all, I’m one person doing three people’s jobs, I really can’t get away. I authorize Chen Xi to represent me fully. I’ll send the electronic copy of the contract to your phone now.”

    “I don’t work for your company,” said Chen Xi.

    “Then represent yourself.”

    The call ended.

    4. The Mediation Room

    The mediation room was on the first floor of the sub-district office.

    A room of twenty-odd square metres, a long table with four chairs on each side, the table covered in dark green baize under a sheet of glass. On the wall hung a scroll, “Harmony is most precious,” in a glass frame with a water stain in one corner. On the windowsill was a pothos, half its leaves yellow.

    The mediator was called Ma, in his sixties; before retiring he had worked at the sub-district office for thirty years, and everyone called him Director Ma. He wore a grey sweater with a navy jacket over it, and pinned to the front of the jacket a badge reading “People’s Mediator.” He poured everyone a cup of tea, the very cheap kind of green tea that brews up yellowish.

    “Sit, everyone, sit,” said Director Ma. “Today we’re not here to argue, we’re here to solve a problem. Family matters are family matters at the end of the day; there’s no knot that can’t be untied.”

    Gu Jianguo and the woman sat on one side. Gu Xuerong and Chen Xi sat on the other. Officer Wang hadn’t come up; he was waiting downstairs. The woman from the sub-district office sat beside Director Ma and opened her notebook.

    The woman said it all again. A little longer than at the neighbourhood committee, and crying a little harder.

    Director Ma heard her out, nodded, and turned to look at Gu Xuerong.

    “Child,” he said, “you heard what your parents said. Your parents mean well for you; there are no parents under heaven who don’t care for their children. You’re a girl, living out there, they worry, that’s only human. Don’t you think perhaps—”

    “She sleeps in the kitchen,” said Chen Xi.

    Director Ma’s words stopped.

    “At home she sleeps in the kitchen, on a folding bed, next to the coal stove, and the coal stove leaks smoke,” said Chen Xi. “The little one sleeps in her own room, with an electric heater in it. On New Year’s Day five of us went, we all saw it. That’s caring for your child? Caring all the way to the kitchen?”

    “You little—” said the woman.

    “Last November, outside No. 8 High, her dad cursed her in the street,” Chen Xi went on. “Cursed her something filthy, I was there, and the four from the internet café were there. Want me to repeat it word for word? I’ve got a loud voice, the police downstairs will hear it too.”

    “That was me disciplining my daughter!” said Gu Jianguo.

    “Disciplining?” Chen Xi leaned back in his chair. “That was you swearing in the street.”

    Director Ma put down the cup in his hand.

    “Young man,” he said, “let me tell you, life isn’t just about being in the right. If you talk like that, when you’re out in the world you’ll come off worst.”

    “Which bit did I get wrong?”

    Director Ma opened his mouth.

    “…You didn’t get it wrong,” he said. “You just shouldn’t say it like that.”

    “Then how should I say it?”

    Director Ma didn’t answer. He picked up his own tea and took a sip; it had gone a bit cold, and he frowned slightly and put it down.

    The woman from the sub-district office wrote a few words in her notebook, then crossed them out.

    “It’s not that we’re being unreasonable.” The woman tried another angle, lowering her voice, with a hint of bargaining in it. “If the child wants to live out, fine. But the money she earns, she ought to give some to the family, oughtn’t she? Her dad carries cement on his own, from dawn to dusk, there’s the little one at home too, it costs a lot. If she earns money and brings some back, to look after her dad, that’s not too much to ask, is it? Director Ma, you tell me, is that too much?”

    Director Ma hesitated, as if this sounded easier to deal with than what came before.

    “Well,” he said, “a child earning money and giving some to the family, that’s filial piety too…”

    “Her dad’s up to his neck in debt,” said Chen Xi.

    The woman’s face went white for a moment.

    “Enzyme drink, the stuff he was selling a few years ago, drink it and it cures everything,” said Chen Xi. “Borrowed money to buy the stock, couldn’t sell it, still owes it now. If you want money to pay off debts, say you want money to pay off debts. Don’t drag filial piety into it.”

    “Who, who told you that nonsense—”

    “She told me herself, in a private chat, typed it out word by word,” said Chen Xi. “Those out-of-date cases in the kitchen, she was the one who unscrewed them bottle by bottle and poured them away. Took her a week.”

    The room went quiet. Gu Jianguo stared at the sheet of glass on the table; the woman clutched the strap of her bag. On the windowsill, a yellow leaf fell from the pothos by itself and landed on the sill with a very faint pat.

    Director Ma looked at one side, then the other.

    “Child,” he finally turned to Gu Xuerong again, “what do you think? You tell us.”

    From the moment she came in, Gu Xuerong had sat in that chair, both hands on her knees, cuffs buttoned. The tea in front of her was untouched and no longer steaming.

    “I want to live on my own,” she said.

    “And the money?” said the woman. “Not a cent of the money for the family?”

    “What else do you want to take from me?” said Gu Xuerong.

    The woman opened her mouth.

    “I have nothing,” said Gu Xuerong. “In your eyes, I’m just a cold stone, it seems.”

    Her hands were still on her knees, cuffs buttoned, not moving.

    “I don’t want to see you. And I haven’t got money for you,” she said. “I don’t want to have the slightest thing to do with you any more.”

    Gu Jianguo shot up from his chair.

    “Is that how a human being talks?!” His voice was so loud the window glass hummed. “Children supporting their parents, that’s the law of heaven! You don’t, and it’s an outrage against heaven and earth! Never mind that I raised you all these years, fed you and clothed you; even if I hadn’t raised you for a single day, you’d still have to support me! So what if I want some money? There’s another one on the way, and you, a worthless girl, you’re nothing compared to the son in this belly!”

    The room went silent.

    The woman’s hand rested on her own belly, her down jacket buttoned up tight, nothing to see. With her other hand she yanked at Gu Jianguo’s sleeve, yanked hard, her nails digging into the fabric.

    Director Ma slowly put down his cup.

    “…How do you know it’s a son?”

    “We had it tested!” said Gu Jianguo. “Took a tube of blood, sent it to Hong Kong, they say it’s really accurate, a hundred per—”

    “Shut up!” The woman pinched his arm hard.

    Gu Jianguo shut up.

    The woman from the sub-district office wrote a line in her notebook, and when she had written it, drew a line under it.

    “What are you going on about,” said Chen Xi.

    He didn’t get up; he stayed leaning back in his chair, his eyes on Gu Jianguo.

    “Holding your hand out for money from a kid this age, have you no shame?” he said. “A tube of blood sent to Hong Kong, a few thousand yuan, there’s money for that. Your daughter sleeping in the kitchen, an electric heater, no money for that.”

    Gu Jianguo glared at him, the veins in his neck standing out one by one, and in the end said nothing, and dropped back into his seat.

    At his end of the table, Director Ma cleared his throat.

    “Well…” he said, “I think we’ll leave it there for today.” He glanced at the woman from the sub-district office. “Mediation depends on both sides being willing. Today it looks like the two sides are still quite far apart. We won’t sign any agreement yet; everyone go home, calm down, think it over. If anything comes up, you can come back.”

    “And the child?” said the woman. “The child just stays out there?”

    “The child is sixteen,” said Director Ma. “She has a job, an income, somewhere to live. If she doesn’t want to go back, we can’t tie her up and take her back.” He paused, as if this was something he didn’t really want to say. “That’s what the law says.”

    Gu Jianguo stood up, his chair scraping loudly across the floor.

    “Fine.” He pointed at Gu Xuerong. “You’re fine. Too big for your boots now. Let’s see how long you last out there.”

    The woman stood up after him, picked up her bag from the sofa, walked to the door, and turned back.

    “Xuerong,” she said, her voice gone soft again, softening very fast, “if you change your mind, call home. Your sister asks every day when big sister’s coming back.”

    The door closed.

    Downstairs, Officer Wang was still there. He stood on the steps outside the sub-district office holding his thermos cup, and when Gu Jianguo and the woman came out he nodded and said nothing. When they had gone some way, and Gu Xuerong and Chen Xi came down, he called them over.

    “About the address,” he said, “I didn’t tell them. I’ve had a word with the community too: whoever comes asking, they don’t give it out.”

    “Thanks,” said Chen Xi.

    Officer Wang took a card from his vest pocket, a police contact card printed with the station’s address and duty number, a mobile number written on the back in biro.

    “If he blocks your way on the street again,” he handed the card to Gu Xuerong, “curses you, follows you, call this. Don’t wait.”

    Gu Xuerong took it, glanced at it, and put it in the pocket of her down jacket.

    “This classmate of yours,” said Officer Wang, looking at Chen Xi, “has a sharp tongue.”

    “Mm.”

    “Sharp,” said Officer Wang, “but he cursed with good reason.”

    He unscrewed his thermos cup, took a sip, and went back inside.

    5. The Card

    The rural commercial bank closed at half past three.

    They got there at five past three. There was hardly anyone in the hall, just an old woman jabbing at the ticket machine and getting nothing out of it. The security guard came over and pressed it for her, handed her a little slip, and she held the slip and read the number on it aloud, one character at a time.

    Gu Xuerong took a ticket too. Number seventeen. Only two people waiting ahead of her.

    Behind the counter was a teller in her twenties, in a mask and a face shield with a film of fog on it. She took Gu Xuerong’s ID, swiped it on the machine, and glanced at the screen.

    “A minor,” she said. “Minors need a guardian present to open an account, with the household register.”

    Chen Xi pushed the folder through the slot under the counter.

    “Everything you need is in there,” he said. “Labour contract, proof of income, wage records. Have a look, and if it’s still no, we’ll talk.”

    The teller glanced at him, opened the folder and went through it page by page. At the proof of income she stopped, picked up the phone beside her, dialled a number, and said a few words quietly.

    A few minutes later a man in his forties came out from the back, a “Lobby Manager” badge pinned to his chest, took the folder, went through it again, and asked Gu Xuerong a few questions: which employer she worked for, what she did, how long she had done it, what she was paid, how it was paid. Gu Xuerong answered them one by one, very briefly.

    The lobby manager closed the folder, handed it back to the teller, and nodded.

    “We can do it.”

    The teller began typing on her computer. After a while she asked: “Phone number?”

    Gu Xuerong gave a number.

    “This number’s your own, is it?”

    “Yes.”

    “All the text alerts for this card will go to this number from now on.”

    “Mm.”

    “Set a PIN, six digits.” The teller pushed the little keypad toward her. “Not your birthday, not consecutive numbers.”

    Gu Xuerong looked at the little keypad.

    Chen Xi turned round, his back to her, and looked at the wealth-management advert on the wall at the other end of the hall. In the advert a man in a suit was smiling, and underneath it said “Steady returns, the peace-of-mind choice.”

    The little keypad beeped six times.

    “Enter it again.”

    Six more beeps.

    The printer started humming and spat out a few sheets; the teller had her sign, in four places. Then she took a card from a drawer, blue, printed with the bank’s name and a string of numbers, put it in a white paper sleeve, and pushed it out through the slot.

    “Done,” said the teller. “Next.”

    Gu Xuerong picked up the card, looked at it, and put it in the pocket of her down jacket, together with Officer Wang’s card.

    When they came out of the bank, the sun was already sinking west. The March sun had no strength in it; it shone on the street, on the concrete where the snow had just melted, glaring.

    The two of them walked back. Chen Xi had the half-empty folder under his arm, and as he walked the snap came loose and popped open, and he snapped it shut again.

    At the end of Back Street, Gu Xuerong stopped and looked at the paper on the internet café door. “please open soon begging you,” “+1,” and below that, added at some point, another line:

    “+2 —Huang Yingjun”

    “He put his name on it,” said Gu Xuerong.

    “…Idiot,” said Chen Xi.

    6. The Insulated Pot

    Su Tang came in the evening.
