    She was carrying an insulated food pot, stainless steel, three tiers, a ring of tape wound round the handle, the one her family had used for years. She stood at the cat café door, took off her mask, out of breath, her face red with cold, a smudge of dust from somewhere in her hair.

    “I came on my bike!” she said. “The checkpoint on the bridge over the river came down today, so I came. My mum says you’re eating instant noodles every day, she told me to bring some food.”

    Ye Zhixia sprang up off the sofa.

    The pot opened tier by tier. The top tier was rice, the second braised spare ribs, glossy with sauce, cooked down very dry, and the third a plate of stir-fried choy sum, with two fried eggs, the yolks runny.

    “Sister Su Tang,” said Ye Zhixia, holding her bowl, her words a bit mushy, “you’re a goddess.”

    “Not a goddess, my mum made the ribs, I just did the greens.”

    Ye Zhixing didn’t start eating straight away. He took his bowl to the window and leaned against the sill. Outside it was nearly dark, and the snow on the roof opposite had all melted, showing the grey-black tiles underneath.

    Su Tang went over and stood beside him.

    “Chen Xi told the group,” she said. “About the mediation room.”

    “Mm.”

    “Is Xuerong… OK?”

    “Don’t know,” said Ye Zhixing. “The card got done.”

    Su Tang looked down at the windowsill. There was a ring of white cat fur on it, where Rice Cake usually lay.

    “Ye Zhixing.”

    “Hm?”

    “Are you… really not tired?”

    Ye Zhixing picked up a rib, bit into it, and chewed for a while.

    “I am,” he said.

    Su Tang didn’t seem to have expected him to be that direct, and stopped short.

    “Then today you—”

    “Today in the city,” said Ye Zhixing, “the hotpot owner talked to me for four hours. What he wants changed three times, he pushed the price down twice, and in the end he said thirty per cent up front, the rest depending on results. I said fine. When Chen Xi called, I was in the hotpot place’s kitchen; they were trying out new dishes, someone was chopping ribs.” He took another bite of rib. “About this size.”

    Su Tang didn’t laugh.

    “Then why didn’t you go?” she said. “To the mediation room.”

    “What would I have done there?”

    “…Kept her company.”

    “Chen Xi was there,” said Ye Zhixing. “Chen Xi’s better at talking than me. If I’d gone, her dad would have seen me and said ‘that’s the rich family’s young master who’s been seducing my daughter.’ And everyone in that room would have thought so.”

    Su Tang swallowed what she was going to say. She put her hands in the pockets of her down jacket, kept them there a while, then took them out again.

    “Ye Zhixing,” she said, “do you… like Xuerong?”

    “You’re the second person to ask me that.”

    “Who was the first?”

    Ye Zhixing pointed his chopsticks toward the sofa. Ye Zhixia was bent over the coffee table gnawing a rib, grease all over her face, and Rice Cake was crouched beside her, eyes glued to her bowl.

    Su Tang let out a “pfft” of laughter, and quickly stopped.

    “Then if you do,” she said, “why not just tell her?”

    “It’s not that,” said Ye Zhixing. “What I feel about her isn’t only that kind of thing.”

    He put his bowl down on the windowsill.

    “Honestly,” he said, “I don’t know if I still have the right to fall for anyone.”

    “Why?”

    “Before…” he paused, “before, I let a lot of people down. A lot. I don’t want them to look at me like that. You know? That kind of… the way they look at you.”

    Su Tang looked at him.

    She didn’t understand. She didn’t know when “before” was, who “a lot of people” were, what “the way they look at you” looked like. But she looked at his profile, and when he said “a lot,” the muscle along his jaw moved.

    “…Mm,” she said.

    “Don’t ask.”

    “I wasn’t going to.”

    “It’s written all over your face.”

    “What’s written on my face is my face’s business,” said Su Tang. “My mouth didn’t ask.”

    Ye Zhixing turned his head and looked at her face, screwed up in its effort to be serious, and laughed.

    “Who did you learn that from.”

    “Xuerong,” said Su Tang.

    “I just think,” said Su Tang, “you’re the kind of person who buries himself really deep. You carry everything yourself. Your family, Xuerong, the company, the cats, Zhixia. Why do you have to carry it all on your own?”

    “Who else would carry it?”

    “Other…” Su Tang thought for a moment. “Other people. Hand some out.” She drew a finger through the ring of cat fur on the sill. “Is there anything I can help with?”

    Ye Zhixing switched his bowl to his other hand.

    “I know my family isn’t well off,” said Su Tang, “and I don’t understand all your stuff, companies, economics, finance, haha…” She gave a couple of dry laughs, a little awkward. “I only found out what Yu’e Bao was last year. But I haven’t got the pressure you’ve got. My mum and dad are fine, my brothers are annoying but they’re fine. There’s lots of empty space in my head, room for things. The things you talk about, I can learn. I don’t understand them now, I’ll understand them later.”

    Ye Zhixing looked out of the window. A pigeon landed on the roof opposite, walked a few steps on the tiles, and flew off again.

    “The county town’s economy,” he said, “might be in trouble soon.”

    “What trouble?”

    “Houses,” said Ye Zhixing. “The kind my family does. Too many built, fewer and fewer people buying, all the money buried in land, buried in buildings. And now the epidemic’s here, nobody dares spend money. Those buildings of my dad’s, in a year or two, they might—” He didn’t finish. “The county town’s only this big. If my family goes down, it won’t be only my family that goes down.”

    Su Tang didn’t really follow, but she understood the words “goes down.”

    “So what do you do?”

    “Leave,” said Ye Zhixing. “Can’t stay here for ever. Have to get somewhere bigger. Somewhere more open.”

    “Where?”

    “A big city,” he said. “Maybe… do something in finance.”

    Su Tang looked at him.

    “Finance?”

    “Mm.”

    “Didn’t you say your family was exactly—”

    “That’s why I know how it dies,” said Ye Zhixing.

    He picked up the bowl from the windowsill again; the rice had gone a bit cold. He shovelled in a mouthful.

    “You said you wanted to learn,” he said through the rice, indistinctly. “Then first work out Yu’e Bao.”

    “I have worked it out!”

    “Then tell me, where does the money in Yu’e Bao come from?”

    “…From my phone.”

    Ye Zhixing laughed out loud, nearly spraying rice, and clamped a hand over his mouth.

    “What are you laughing at!” Su Tang’s face went red. “Then you tell me where it comes from!”

    “I’ll explain tomorrow.”

    “Explain now!”

    “Now we eat.”

    By the time they got back to the coffee table, the second tier of the insulated pot was empty.

    Rice Cake was crouched beside the pot, a ring of grease round its mouth, licking its paws. Ye Zhixia was at the other end of the sofa clutching her bowl, two ribs still left in it, guarding it with one hand and shouting at Rice Cake:

    “You stole again! You stole again! You just ate a whole bag of freeze-dried!”

    Rice Cake finished its left paw and moved on to its right.

    “When did it steal it?” Su Tang asked.

    “Just now! I went to get a glass of water, and when I came back—” Ye Zhixia pointed at the pot. “It pushed the lid off! Sister Su Tang, it can open lids!”

    Su Tang looked at the empty second tier, at Rice Cake’s greasy face.

    “…Rice Cake,” she crouched down, “that was for people.”

    Rice Cake burped.

    Ye Zhixia pulled the “Criminal Record” off the coffee table and added another line at the bottom of Rice Cake’s column, writing very hard: 18 March, stole Sister Su Tang’s family’s braised spare ribs, about five pieces.

    Chapter Eighteen

    Empty Bottles

    6,687 words · about 29 min

    1. Masks

    Su Tang logged on at eight every morning.

    The customer-service back end was a web page: a column of conversations on the left, the chat box on the right, and along the top a row of red numbers, the unanswered messages. She propped her phone on a stack of textbooks on her desk; the computer was her dad’s old laptop, which took three minutes to boot and whose fan sounded like a hairdryer when it got going. While her two brothers were in their online classes, the computer was hers.

    The messages on Town Matters were different from when the epidemic was at its worst. Fewer requests for help, more questions. Which barber’s had reopened, when could you book a driving test, which corner had the old man who sold vegetables outside the estate moved to, could someone post a transfer, a pram, ninety per cent new, baby grew too fast.

    And there was one woman who sent a message at ten every morning on the dot: Still no eating in today?

    Every day Su Tang replied: Not yet~ waiting for the notice~

    Every day the woman replied with a crying face.

    Later Su Tang found out the woman ran a noodle shop opposite the county hospital, had run it for eleven years, and the pot of bone broth at the door had never once been off the boil. Now the fire had been out for two months.

    Her parents’ attitude to this job started out as “signing a contract is a good thing,” and slowly turned into something else.

    When her mum came home from work every day—the textile mill had reopened at half capacity last week, and her mum was on the day shift—the first thing she said coming in was “Tired today?”, and the second was “How’s your boss doing?” When her dad watched the news and saw some company laying people off, some factory stopping work, he called her over and pointed at the TV and said, see, your company’s doing all right, isn’t it?

    “It’s all right.”

    “Good. You work hard there, get on well with the boss.”

    “I know.”

    “So young, holding up a whole show like that on his own,” said her dad. “Don’t just take the wages, if there’s anything you can help with, help.”

    And then they started stuffing things into her bag.

    First a pot of steamed flower rolls her mum made; her mum said she’d made too many, they couldn’t finish them, take them to your boss. Then two cases of milk her dad’s work had handed out; her dad said he didn’t like milk, take them. Then a jar of spicy pickled cabbage, the kind her grandma, when she was alive, had taught her mum to make by hand, this year’s crock nearly at the bottom, the very last of it; her mum hesitated for ages, then packed one container of it after all.

    “Tell him not to wear himself out.” Her mum pressed the lid of the container down, then pressed it again. “Young people staying up all night, they don’t feel it now, but it all has to be paid back later.”

    “Mum, he doesn’t listen to me.”

    “Then say it a few more times.”

    “…”

    “And,” said her mum, “when school starts, no letting it get in the way of lessons. Work is work, study is study. If you drop out of the top fifty in the midterm, you’re giving up this job.”

    “I know.”

    “If you know, what are you standing there for? Go.”

    On the bridge over the river, now the checkpoint was gone, you had to wear a mask to cross, and at the end of the bridge stood an old man in a red armband who shouted at anyone without one. Su Tang rode her old bike with the flower rolls and the cabbage in the basket and a case of milk tied to the back with string, her mask on tight, and as she crossed the bridge the wind got in round the edges of the mask and made her eyes stream.

    There were a few more people on Back Street than last week. The copy shop was open; the braised-meat stall wasn’t out yet. The internet café’s curtain was hooked up, and two boys stood at the door in masks smoking, masks pulled down under their chins: a drag, mask up, another drag, mask down.

    On the cat café door was a sheet of A4 in Ye Zhixia’s writing, very large:

    Dine-in suspended. Cats are well. Don’t worry.

    Underneath was a drawing of a cat, recognizably Rice Cake, because it was drawn very round.

    Su Tang went up, knocked, and the door opened. The moment she was inside she took off her mask, and the smell of cat fur and cat litter and the dry heat baked out by the electric heater all came rushing at her.

    Ye Zhixing was sitting behind the bar counter, facing his computer.

    He was wearing a grey hoodie, the same one he had on when she came the day before yesterday, a tuft of cat fur stuck to the cuff, which had been stuck there the day before yesterday too. On the counter were three instant-noodle tubs stacked one inside another, the fork still stuck in the top one. He had headphones on, in a meeting; when he heard the door he raised one hand and waved at her, then put it down again, his eyes not leaving the screen.

    “…Right, the button on the second version goes bottom right, not bottom left, there aren’t many left-handers… No, I’m not discriminating against left-handers…”

    Su Tang put the things on the shoe cabinet by the door, and crouched to untie the string round the case of milk from the back of the bike.

    At the start of the school year, she had seen Ye Zhixing. Not at the cat café, but on the No. 8 High sports field, back in the make-up military training. She was in Class Three then, he was in Class Seven, two companies apart. She remembered him standing at attention all crooked, the instructor yelling at him and him not caring, one earbud in his ear and the other hanging on his chest, swinging. He was given ten laps as punishment, and when he’d finished he wasn’t even out of breath; he sat down on the ground, unscrewed a bottle of water, tipped his head back and gulped it, and when he’d gulped it he was still laughing and joking with the people next to him.

    Back then she had thought: so this is the kind of person people talk about. Rich family, nothing to be afraid of.

    She carried the milk in and put it beside the bar counter. Ye Zhixing was still in his meeting; halfway through a sentence he stopped, gave a very long yawn, and when he’d finished yawning carried on.

    2. Chen Xi’s Classes

    Chen Xi had made a fair bit of money.

    He didn’t say exactly how much, but one day he transferred his mum two thousand, and she stood in the kitchen stunned for ages, then came out and asked whether he had stolen it or robbed someone. He said he had earned it teaching. She didn’t believe him, so he showed her a screenshot of the QQ group class, with over a hundred and thirty people in the group. His mum turned his phone over and over in her hands, and in the end transferred a thousand of the two thousand back.

    “A thousand’s enough,” she said. “Keep the rest yourself. Don’t waste it.”

    He didn’t listen.

    With the rest of the money he bought a new pair of trainers, bought three game season passes, and the moment the internet café opened, topped up five hundred on a membership. He also treated the internet café gang to barbecue twice; the barbecue stall had only come out at the end of March, and the owner wore his mask hooked over one ear and coughed as he grilled, coughed so much that Huang Yingjun shifted his stool back half a metre.

    “Xi the Great’s treat,” said Abiao, holding up a skewer of kidney.

    “Say that again and I’ll kick you.”

    “You kick people from the group, not from the barbecue stall.”

    Chen Xi thought about it, decided that was fair, and said nothing more, and picked up a chicken wing.

    He taught differently from other people.

    Everyone who had been to his classes knew that, but nobody could quite say how. A girl from Class Three once said in the group: “Mr. Chen doesn’t explain problems, he takes them apart.”

    That evening the topic was logarithms.

    The few lessons on logarithms last term, more than half the class hadn’t understood; when online classes stopped and they dug them out to revise, they still couldn’t understand them, and asked in the group. Chen Xi said fine, I’ll explain, nothing else to do in the evening anyway.

    “Forget logarithms for now,” he said. “Let me ask you: what is addition?”

    The group was quiet for a few seconds.

    “And multiplication? Multiplication is a shortcut for addition. Three times four is three plus three plus three plus three, four threes added up; you couldn’t be bothered to add them one by one, so you invented multiplication.

    “Powers are a shortcut for multiplication. Three to the fourth is three times three times three times three. You couldn’t be bothered to multiply them one by one, so you invented powers.

Addition backwards is subtraction, multiplication backwards is division, powers backwards—there are two directions. You know the base and the exponent and ask for the result: that’s a power.     3. The Basement

    It was Su Tang’s first time at the place where Gu Xuerong lived.

    She knew Xuerong had a “place,” Lin Xiaoman knew, everyone knew, but nobody had ever been. The trip to the urban village at New Year had been to the Gu family’s. This place was Gu Xuerong’s own.

    Gu Xuerong had sent the location herself. The night before, in MC, Su Tang had said hasn’t your place gone a long time without a tidy, and Gu Xuerong said “don’t know,” and Su Tang said then I’ll come and help you tidy tomorrow, and after a long gap Gu Xuerong typed two words in the chat bar: “if you like.”

    Then she sent a location.

    Two turns in from Back Street, the side of an old building. Su Tang stood there looking at the seven steps going down; at the bottom was an iron door, most of its paint gone, rusted out in reddish-brown patches. Beside the door was a little window with its sill level with the pavement; she looked down at it, and the glass was coated in a layer of dust, so she couldn’t see inside.

    She had her mask on and was carrying a big plastic bag with bin bags, rubber gloves, cloths, a bottle of washing-up liquid, a bottle of 84 disinfectant, and a bag of tangerines her mum had pushed on her.

    She went down the steps and knocked on the door.

    It was a long time before the door opened. Gu Xuerong stood inside, in that grey thermal set—the one Lin Xiaoman gave her—with a very old sweater over it, her hair not tied, a tangled mess round her shoulders.

    “…You came.”

    “I came!” said Su Tang, her voice a bit muffled through the mask.

    She went in and took off her mask.

    Then she stood in the doorway, stunned.

    It was very dark inside, only a little grey light from the small window. Gu Xuerong reached out and pulled the thin cord by the door, and the bulb overhead came on, bare, a yellow glow.

    The room wasn’t big, ten-odd square metres. A single bed against the wall, the quilt on it bundled into a heap. A table, with a computer on it, and beside the computer an electric pot with half a pot of noodle soup of unknown age in it, a layer of white fat set on top. In the corner the blue-and-white checked cloth was still covering something, a square bulge, so you couldn’t tell what it was. Against the wall stood the little fridge, and stuck on the fridge door was a sticky note in handwriting Su Tang recognized, Ye Zhixing’s: Don’t unplug.

    And then there were the bottles.

    Bottles all over the floor. Coke, Sprite, Fanta, iced tea, orange juice, bottle after bottle, empty, lying every which way on the floor, leaning in the corners, piled at the foot of the bed, under the table too, some with the caps screwed on, some not, some with a bit left in the bottom gone a strange colour. Instant-noodle tubs and packets were mixed in among the bottles, some of the seasoning sachets torn open, some not.

    “Xuerong…” said Su Tang, “these… you drank all these?”

    “Mm.”

    “Over how long?”

    “New Year till now.”

    Su Tang looked down at a Coke bottle by her foot. Two-litre, empty, the body crushed halfway and sprung back a little.

    “How many bottles a day do you drink?”

    “Don’t know,” said Gu Xuerong. “When I’m thirsty I drink.”

    “Do you drink water?”

    “This is water.”

    Su Tang opened her mouth, and nothing came out.

    She put the plastic bag on the floor, took out a pair of rubber gloves, put them on, took out a big black bin bag, and shook it open.

    “Let’s go!”

    Halfway through the tidying, Su Tang found a plastic bag under the bed.

    The bag was tied shut, tied very tight; she undid it and looked inside: a duck carcass, every scrap of meat long gone from the bones, dried and yellowed, and beside it a few pear cores, shrivelled into little blackish-brown lumps.

    “What’s this?”

    Gu Xuerong was pulling bottles out from under the table, heard, and poked her head out to look.

    “New Year’s Eve dinner.”

    “…What?”

    “What I ate at New Year,” said Gu Xuerong. “Instant noodles, roast duck, pears.”

    “Where did the roast duck come from?”

    “The braised-meat stall on Back Street. Bought it the day before the lockdown. It was his last day out, he was selling cheap, twenty for a whole one.”

    “Just you, on your own?”

    “Mm.”

    “Then you…” Su Tang crouched by the bed, holding the plastic bag, “pears at New Year? Pear, li, sounds like parting, you’re not supposed to eat pears at New Year, sharing a pear means splitting up—”

    “They were cheap,” said Gu Xuerong. “One-fifty a jin.”

    For a moment Su Tang didn’t know what to say.

    Gu Xuerong reached an iced-tea bottle out from under the table and threw it into the bin bag, where it clanged against the other bottles.

    “I haven’t got anyone to part from,” she said.

    Su Tang tied the plastic bag up again, tied it very tight, and threw it into the bin bag.

    The bottles filled four big bags. The noodle tubs filled one. Su Tang poured the half pot of noodle soup down the toilet and flushed it, scrubbed the electric pot three times, until the black scorched mark on the bottom had at last faded a little. She swept, mopped, diluted the 84 with water and wiped down the corners and under the bed.

    The thing under the cloth, Su Tang didn’t touch. When she got there with her cloth, she went round it.

    Gu Xuerong was tidying too, but very slowly. Bend once, pick up a bottle, straighten up, rest a while, bend again. Su Tang watched her and said nothing, only went a little faster herself.

    When they had finished it was nearly noon. The two of them sat on the edge of the bed; the sheet had been changed, for the one Su Tang had brought, an old sheet her mum had dug out, blue-and-white check, washed a little pale.

    Su Tang peeled a tangerine and gave half to Gu Xuerong.

    Gu Xuerong took it and held it, and didn’t eat.

    “Xuerong.”

    “Mm.”

    “Before…” said Su Tang, “before, when you watched all that scary stuff, those games, those films. The first time I watched I threw up, remember? I’ve always wanted to ask you, how come you’re not scared?”

    Gu Xuerong looked down at the half tangerine in her hand.

    “When I was in middle school,” she said, “she showed me films.”

    “Who?”

    “Auntie.”

    “…She showed you horror films?”

    “Not horror films,” said Gu Xuerong. “The kind… about hell.”

    She spoke very slowly, a sentence at a time, as if thinking how to put it.

    “There’s a kind of painting called the transformations of hell. It shows people after they die, going down to hell, the Ten Kings, judged by one court after another. Mountains of knives, pots of boiling oil, tongues pulled out, sawn in half. Painted in a lot of detail. She bought a big one at a temple fair and stuck it on the kitchen wall. Right across from my bed.

    “And discs. From the temple fair too, ten yuan for three. About karma, about what you owed someone in a past life, you have to pay back in this one. One was about karmic creditors. It said there are four kinds of children: the ones come to repay kindness, the ones come for revenge, the ones come to collect a debt, the ones come to pay a debt. The debt-collecting kind are born just to take money; in a past life you owed them, so in this life they’re born into your family and take your family’s money cent by cent, and when they’ve taken it all, they leave.”

    Su Tang’s hand stopped in mid-air.

    “She made you watch that?”

    “Mm,” said Gu Xuerong. “She said I’m the debt-collecting kind.”

    “…”

    “She said, look, ever since you came, this family’s had bad luck. Your dad’s business lost money, he can’t pay back what he borrowed, that’s all you collecting.”

    Su Tang put down her half tangerine.

    “But… but that was your dad himself—”

    “I know,” said Gu Xuerong. “He bought the enzyme drink himself.”

    She broke a segment off her half tangerine, put it in her mouth, chewed, swallowed.

    “That painting stayed up there,” she said. “Every night when I went to sleep, the moment I opened my eyes there it was. I looked at it for three years. After that, nothing scared me. Those things in the games, next to that painting, they’re all quite good-looking.”

    Su Tang said nothing. She looked at Gu Xuerong’s profile, at the way she chewed the tangerine, very slowly, one bite after another, as if chewing something perfectly ordinary.

    “She believes in another thing too,” said Gu Xuerong. “It’s called Three Redemptions Christ.”

    “…What?”

    “Three Redemptions Christ,” said Gu Xuerong. “Some people call it the Disciples’ Association. A few women from the village meet at one of their houses every week, door shut, chanting, singing. They say when you’re ill you don’t need medicine, pray and you’ll get better. They say in a few years there’ll be a great flood, believers will be saved and everyone else will drown.”

    “Isn’t that… isn’t that a cult?”

    “Mm.”

    “One’s Buddhist and one’s Christian,” said Su Tang. “How can she… believe both?”

    “She believes all of them,” said Gu Xuerong. “Whichever one says it’ll help her have a son, she believes that one.”

    Su Tang’s mouth hung open.

    “That time I had a fever,” said Gu Xuerong, “in the second year of middle school, over thirty-nine. She wouldn’t let me take medicine, she made me kneel in the kitchen and listen to her chant. She chanted all night.”

    “…And then?”

    “Then it went down,” said Gu Xuerong. “She said the prayers worked.”

    She ate another segment of tangerine.

    “And now she’s pregnant,” said Su Tang, her voice shaking a little, “if she won’t go to hospital—”

    “She will,” said Gu Xuerong. “It’s a son in there.”

    Su Tang sat on the edge of that bed for a long time.

    She thought of her mum. Her mum believed in things a bit too: burned incense at New Year, went to the temple on the first and fifteenth to kowtow. When she was little and had a fever, her mum went to the temple for a charm too and stuck it at the head of her bed. But after she got the charm, her mum still carried her to the county hospital, went to A&E, sat up all night in the corridor, and the next day her eyes were swollen like two peaches.

    Her mum had never said she’d come to collect a debt.

    “Xuerong,” she said, “um…”

    “Su Tang.”

    “Hm?”

    “Why do you bother with me?”

    Su Tang was taken aback.

    Gu Xuerong put the remaining few segments of tangerine on the sheet in a row, one segment against the next.

    “Just leave me like this,” she said. “Look, I’m quite fine like this. I’ve got food, I’ve got drink, I’ve got a computer, I’ve got somewhere to sleep.”

    “This is quite fine?”

    “Mm.”

    “Bottles all over the floor is quite fine?”

    “You threw all the bottles away.”

    Su Tang was stumped.

    “I know what you want to say,” said Gu Xuerong. “You want to say, be a bit happier.”

    She moved the row of tangerine segments, lining them up straighter.

    “But being happy seems like a really hard thing,” she said. “I don’t know how to do it. I look at you lot, you, Xiaoman, Chen Xi, it’s like you were born knowing how. You laugh, you cry, you argue, you’re happy. I watch, and I feel…”

    She thought for a moment, looking for the word.

    “Envious,” she said. “I envy you. Maybe people are just born different.”

    “That’s not—”

    “Maybe,” said Gu Xuerong. “Maybe my whole life I’m just a heap of mud.”

    Su Tang’s nose stung all at once.

    “Don’t say that…”

    “I’m not sad,” said Gu Xuerong. “I mean it. I don’t know what scared is, and I don’t know what hurting is. It’s like… I can’t feel those things. The feelings other people talk about, that love, I can’t feel it either. I don’t know what they’re like.”

    She turned her head and looked at Su Tang.

    “So you don’t need to bother with me,” she said. “If you do, I won’t feel it anyway.”

    Su Tang’s eyes were already red, tears going round in them, round twice, not falling. She sniffed, grabbed the row of tangerine segments in one hand, and pushed them back into Gu Xuerong’s hand.

    “Eat them,” she said.

    “…”

    “Eat them!”

    Gu Xuerong looked down at the tangerine in her hand and ate a segment.

    “Xuerong, listen to me,” said Su Tang. Her voice was shaking, but she didn’t let it shake too much. “I don’t know what you mean by not being able to feel. I’m stupid, I don’t understand those things. But I know one thing: however hard it gets, you have to keep living.”

    Gu Xuerong chewed her tangerine and made no sound.

    “Between people,” said Su Tang, “whatever happens, you have to help each other. You help me, I help you. If you can’t help me now, that’s fine, you help later. If you can’t help later either, that’s fine, I still help you. That’s just what I think. Whatever the problem, it can be solved in the end. I believe that.”

    “…You believing it,” said Gu Xuerong, “doesn’t mean it can be solved.”

    “Then I’ll keep believing it, until it’s solved!”

    Gu Xuerong didn’t answer.

    Su Tang sniffed, wiped her eyes with her sleeve, and then—she didn’t know how herself—split into a grin. A very ugly grin, the tears still hanging there, her nose bright red.

    “Smile a bit,” she said. “You smile a bit too.”

    “…”

    “Stop watching all that scary stuff, OK? That stupid painting’s not across from your bed any more. What’s across from your bed now?”

    Gu Xuerong turned her head and looked across from the bed. Across from the bed was the little window, its sill level with the pavement, and outside it a pair of feet went by in pink trainers, flap, flap.

    “…The window.”

    “Yes! The window!” said Su Tang. “People walk past outside! There’s sun! That painting’s gone! Just feel it a bit, there are good things in this world, there’s love, there are people who are good to you—”

    “You,” said Gu Xuerong.

    Su Tang stopped dead.

    “…Huh?”

    “People who are good to me,” said Gu Xuerong. “You said. That’s you.”

    Su Tang’s tears finally fell, two big ones at once, splashing onto the blue-and-white checked sheet.

    “Yes,” she said, “it’s me. And Xiaoman, and Chen Xi, and… and loads of people.” She wiped her eyes again. “Whatever happens, I’m here. I said so. Remember it.”

    Gu Xuerong looked at her.

    At her red nose, at the tears hanging on her lashes, at that ugly wide grin.

    “When you cry,” said Gu Xuerong, “your nose runs.”

    “…Xuerong!!”

    4. A Body Full of Cats

    That afternoon, Su Tang carried the four big bags of bottles and threw them one by one into the rubbish point at the end of Back Street. Crouched beside the rubbish point was an old man who collected scrap, in a grey cloth mask, and when he saw her throwing bottles away he jumped up and said don’t throw them, don’t throw them, give them to me.

    So Su Tang gave him all the bottles.

    The old man stamped them flat one by one, crunch, crunch, and when he’d stamped them he put them into his own woven sack. Four big bags took him nearly twenty minutes. When he was done, he took two yuan out of his pocket and tried to give it to her.

    “No, no—”

    “Take it!” said the old man. “That many bottles, they’re worth something!”

    Su Tang stood at the rubbish point holding the two yuan, not knowing what to do. In the end she put the two yuan in her pocket, thinking next time she’d buy Xuerong a bottle of water. Real water.

    When she got to the cat café, it was nearly six.

    Ye Zhixia opened the door. She was wearing the beige apron, covered in cat fur, holding a lint roller, and when she saw Su Tang her eyes lit up, then dimmed.

    “Sister Su Tang.” She lowered her voice. “You’ve come at just the right time.”

    “What is it?”

    Ye Zhixia jerked her chin toward the bar counter.

    Ye Zhixing was still sitting there. Same grey hoodie, same position, facing his computer, the light of the screen on his face, which was a bluish white. The noodle tubs on the counter had gone from three to four.

    “He hasn’t slept,” said Ye Zhixia, “since yesterday morning.”

    “…What?”

    “He got up yesterday morning and started on it, worked till the middle of the night, when I went to sleep he was working, when I got up he was still working,” said Ye Zhixia. “At noon I made him a bowl of noodles, he ate two mouthfuls and left it, it’s all mush now. I tell him to sleep and he says ‘mm, in a minute,’ he’s said it eight times.”

    Su Tang went over.

    Close up, she could see his eyes were full of red veins, two dark bluish-black marks under them. The screen had several windows open: one of code, one a spreadsheet, one a chat app with a dozen conversations flashing, and one the Town Matters back end, the number in its top right corner red.

    “Ye Zhixing.”

    “Mm.” He didn’t look up. “Su Tang, you’re here. I ate the spicy cabbage, it’s good. Thank your mum for me.”

    “That was this morning.”

    “Hm?”

    “The spicy cabbage was this morning. It’s six in the evening now.”

    Ye Zhixing raised his head and glanced out of the window. Outside it was already dark, the tiles on the roof opposite black.

    “…Oh.”

    “How long since you slept?”

    “Not long.”

    “Zhixia says you haven’t slept since yesterday morning.”

    Ye Zhixing glanced over at the sofa. Ye Zhixia, holding Rice Cake, stood by the sofa with a so-I-told-on-you-what-of-it face.

    “That hotpot place,” said Ye Zhixing, “they’ve changed what they want again, they want to see the first version next Monday. Big Liu’s putting new levels into the mini-game, and Huang Yingjun’s stuff needs me to look at it. Town Matters has had a jump in posts these last two days, lots of places are reopening, they all want to post jobs, and the review side—”

    “Sister Xiaowen’s reviewing.”

    “Xiaowen can’t keep up on her own—”

    “I was reviewing this afternoon too,” said Su Tang. “At Xuerong’s, on my phone. I did over forty.”

    Ye Zhixing stopped short.

    “…Weren’t you going to help her tidy her place?”

    “Finished,” said Su Tang. “When I finished I reviewed. I’m fast.”

    Ye Zhixing opened his mouth as if to say something, and didn’t. He turned back to the screen and put his hands on the keyboard, but didn’t type.

    “Ye Zhixing,” said Su Tang, “are you really not tired?”

    “I am.”

    “Then sleep.”

    “Can’t sleep.”

    “You haven’t even lain down, how do you know you can’t sleep?”

    Ye Zhixing ignored her, swiped a finger on the touchpad, and dragged one window behind another.

    “Ye Zhixing.”

    “…”

    “I’m talking to you.”

    “You don’t understand at all.”

    When he said it, his voice wasn’t loud, and he didn’t look at her.

    Su Tang stood there, taken aback.

    “It’s that I don’t dare,” said Ye Zhixing. “I don’t dare let go of that breath. The moment I let go, something falls. The company falls, Town Matters falls, Big Liu’s family, Xiaowen, the two street promoters, you, Xuerong, Huang Yingjun, I brought all of them in. The moment I let go, they—”

    He stopped.

    “I don’t understand,” said Su Tang, “but you never told me either.”

    Ye Zhixing didn’t answer.

    “You don’t say anything,” said Su Tang. “You don’t talk about your family, you don’t talk about three years ago, you don’t say you’re tired, you don’t say when you’re hurting. You just keep going and keep going, getting everything right, thinking of everything. You think people can’t see?”

    “So what if they see,” said Ye Zhixing. “Real life isn’t solved by people seeing it.”

    He took his hands off the keyboard, leaned back in his chair, tipped his head back, and looked at the ceiling. The pendant lamp on the ceiling had a rattan shade Uncle He had bought when the cat café opened, now covered in a layer of cat fur.

    “I live like a machine,” he said, “think of everything, look after everyone, work out every step.” He pulled up one corner of his mouth. “Not because I’m good at it. Because I don’t want to get it wrong again.”

    “Again?”

    “…”

    “You got it wrong before?”

    Ye Zhixing didn’t answer.

    He kept his head tipped back, staring at that fur-covered lamp, until Su Tang thought he had fallen asleep with his eyes open. Su Tang stood beside him and didn’t hurry him. Ye Zhixia, holding Rice Cake, stood by the sofa, and didn’t make a sound either.

    “I don’t know how to say it,” he said at last. “And if I said it you’d…” He shook his head. “Forget it. A life is long. And pretty dull. You walk alone, you work alone. That’s it.”

    When he’d said it, he seemed to think himself that it was too gloomy, sat up, and reached for the mouse again.

    Su Tang slammed his laptop shut.

    Smack.

    Ye Zhixing looked at the closed laptop, then at her.

    “…I hadn’t saved.”

    “It autosaves.”

    “How do you know?”

    “I don’t,” said Su Tang. “But you’ve been at it a day and a night, the bit you didn’t save, do it again tomorrow.”

    She grabbed his arm and pulled him up out of the chair. He was a head taller than her, but pulled like that he actually came up, swayed, and steadied himself on the bar counter.

    “See,” said Su Tang, “you can’t even stand.”

    “My legs have gone to sleep.”

    “Then lie down and let them sleep.”

    She dragged him over to the grey sofa and gave him a push. He sat down, and once he was down his whole body tipped back against the sofa, his eyes half open.

    “Just lying down for a bit,” he said. “Twenty minutes. You wake me.”

    “Yes, yes, twenty minutes.”

    “Really wake me.”

    “Really, really.”

    He put his legs up on the sofa and lay down, banging his head on the armrest as he went down, thunk; he hissed, didn’t open his eyes, and just used the armrest as a pillow.

    In less than a minute he was asleep.

    Then the cats came.

    Rice Cake first. It wriggled free of Ye Zhixia’s arms, jumped onto the sofa, trod a few circles on Ye Zhixing’s stomach, so that he grunted in his sleep, and then settled down, curled into a ginger-and-white ball, weighing on the pit of his stomach.

    Then Calico, down from the back of the sofa, burrowing into the gap between his arm and his body, squeezing until the gap was a bit bigger, and lying in it.

    Then the Devon. The Devon had always felt the cold, and in winter went looking for the warmest spot. It sniffed at the side of Ye Zhixing’s neck, smelled something, its big ears twitched, and then it curled up in the hollow of his neck, its head resting on his collarbone.

    Blue-and-White jumped up and lay on his shins. The American Shorthair lay on his feet. The British Blue turned three circles on his knees, couldn’t find a spot, and in the end lay down on top of Blue-and-White, who didn’t object.

    Your Highness came last. It walked out through the sliding door to the back room—which it had opened itself—came to the sofa, looked up, looked at the pile of cats, looked at the person underneath, and then jumped up onto the back of the sofa and lay down in the spot above Ye Zhixing’s head, its long tail hanging down so it rested exactly across his forehead.

    Ye Zhixing slept deeply, not moving at all.

    “…He’s warm,” Ye Zhixia whispered. “They always go for warm places.”

    “How many are there?”

    Ye Zhixia counted. “Seven,” she said. “Briquette won’t come, Briquette only cuddles Sister Xuerong. And the three strays, they’re timid, they don’t dare come over.”

    Su Tang crouched by the sofa, looking at the person buried under seven cats. His face was showing, half hidden by the Devon’s big ears, Your Highness’s tail across his forehead. The two bluish-black marks under his eyes showed even more clearly in the electric heater’s orange-red glow.

    “Sister Su Tang,” said Ye Zhixia, “it’s been twenty minutes, are you going to wake him?”

    “No.”

    “You promised him.”

    “I promised to wake him,” said Su Tang. “I didn’t say when.”

    Ye Zhixia thought about it, and decided the logic was sound.

    Su Tang took out her phone and took a photo of the sofa. When she had taken it, she looked at it, and posted it in the group.

    Su Tang: [image]
    Su Tang: he’s asleep!!
    Lin Xiaoman: so many cats!!! let me count one two three four five six seven!!
    Chen Xi: cat tree
    Huang Yingjun: has brother ye been buried by cats
    Chen Xi: why are you in this group
    Huang Yingjun: brother xi you added me
    Chen Xi: …kicked

    After a while, another message popped up in the group.

    Gu Xuerong: wheres briquette
    Su Tang: briquette wont come it only cuddles you
    Su Tang: its sitting on the windowsill looking out the window like its waiting for someone

    Gu Xuerong didn’t reply again.

    Su Tang put her phone back in her pocket and felt the two yuan in there. From the old scrap collector. She took the two yuan out, smoothed them flat, looked at them, folded them up again and put them back.

    Ye Zhixia had already gone to the kitchen to boil water, to make Su Tang a cup of hot milk, from the case her dad’s work had given out.

    The electric heater hummed. On Ye Zhixing’s stomach, Rice Cake purred, rising and falling.

    Chapter Nineteen

    Back to School

    6,536 words · about 28 min

    1. Masks

    No. 8 High started term on the twentieth of April.

    Year Nine and Year Twelve had gone back half a month earlier; Ye Zhixia left on the seventh of April, packed her schoolbag three times the night before, and woke at six the next morning, before her alarm. Years Ten and Eleven had to wait until the twentieth. The notice was posted in the class group on the sixteenth, and Zheng Xin added a long string of instructions after it: for fourteen days before returning, report your temperature daily on the mini-program; on the day you return, show your health code; queue at the school gate to have your temperature taken; wear masks in the classroom at all times; change masks every four hours; bring at least three days’ supply each.

    The last item: once term starts, the normal schedule resumes, eight classes a day, morning and evening study, the old evening classes cancelled.

    The group filled with a row of “!!!”.

    “Fourteen periods down to eight,” Chen Xi said in the small group. “Considerate virus.”

    There was a very long queue at the school gate.

    The queue stretched all the way to the breakfast stall across the road. Each student had to stand a metre from the next; circles had been painted on the ground in red, one after another, and you stood in a circle, and when you moved up one, you stepped into the next circle. At the gate there was a table with two teachers behind it, one with a thermometer gun, one with a register; the gun beeped, a number was read out, 36.3, 36.5, 36.1, and the register got a tick.

    At Ye Zhixia’s school, they said, you also had to wash your hands: a row of taps just inside the gate, and you had to scrub for a full twenty seconds before they let you in. No. 8 High didn’t have that; at No. 8 High’s gate there was just a bottle of hand sanitizer, one pump, rub, in you go.

    Everyone wore a mask. Mostly blue surgical ones, some white, some black, a few girls in pink ones printed with little flowers, and one boy in an N95, the metal strip over his nose pressed down tight, his voice coming out muffled.

    The desks in the classroom had been pulled apart: before it had been two to a desk, now it was one each, with a bit of space in front, behind and to the sides. Forty-odd desks packed the classroom full; the back row was pushed right up against the blackboard newspaper.

    In the first lesson of term, a director from the academic affairs office came and stood at the front and spoke about discipline for twenty minutes.

    Boys’ hair not past the eyebrows at the front, not past the ears at the sides, not past the collar at the back. Girls with hair past the shoulders must tie it up, not wear it loose, no perms, no dye. No long nails, no nail varnish. No sleeping in class, no putting your head on the desk. No phones in the classroom: caught once, confiscated; caught twice, parents called in; caught three times—

    “Advised to leave,” said the director. “Special circumstances during the epidemic, school management has to be stricter. You’ve had three months off, you’ve all gone wild, now it’s time to rein it in. Anyone who doesn’t want to be here doesn’t have to be; there are plenty of people behind you who’d like to get in.”

    A boy in the back row whose hair was clearly past his eyebrows pulled his mask up a bit, as if that would cover his fringe too.

    2. Chinese Class

    In the first week of term, almost every class had someone getting dealt with.

    Three months of online classes at home: you attended, then you stopped attending; you attended, then you fell asleep. Body clocks were long since wrecked, two or three in the morning to bed, up at noon, and now you had to be at school by six-thirty, with morning reading at seven, and halfway through the reading heads started drooping. People held out through the first lesson; in the second lesson someone put their head down; by the third a whole patch of heads were down.

    The physics teacher threw chalk. He threw very accurately, hitting the back of the head with a smack; whoever was hit jerked upright, and the people beside him held in their laughter. Ms. Li in maths didn’t throw things; Ms. Li made people stand to listen, stand out in the corridor, and after a whole lesson there was a line of them out there, like a row of telegraph poles being punished. The chemistry teacher made people copy out equations, a hundred times. Zheng Xin in English said nothing at all; she walked to the sleeper’s desk, tapped twice lightly on it, and when they raised their head said “go and wash your face,” and walked away.

    Chen Xi was back in class too. The lab had stayed locked since term started; Mr. Wu said no crowding into one room during the epidemic, the competition classes would stop for now, and he sent the two of them back to their class. Chen Xi came back. Ye Zhixing didn’t.

    None of these teachers could deal with Chen Xi.

    Not because Chen Xi didn’t sleep. Chen Xi slept too, more soundly than anyone. But the physics teacher had only just thrown a piece of chalk at him when Chen Xi raised his head and rubbed his eyes; the teacher told him to come up and do a problem, he went up, did it, all correct, and wrote alongside it a method the teacher hadn’t taught; when he’d written it he tossed the chalk, went back to his seat, and went back to sleep.

    Ms. Li made him stand in the corridor. He stood; halfway through, Ms. Li came out to spot-check and asked him where the lesson had got to, and he said the third step of the second example, you wrote the sign the wrong way round in that step. Ms. Li went back and looked at the board, and she really had written it the wrong way round.

    After that nobody bothered with him.

    Except the Chinese teacher.

    The Chinese teacher was called Yang, in her fifties, a woman who had taught for nearly thirty years, wore gold-rimmed glasses, and spoke with a bit of a southern Henan accent, landing hard on every “de.” She was the only teacher in the year who dared point a finger in Chen Xi’s face and tell him off.

    That day it was “Moonlight over the Lotus Pond,” a revision lesson. Ms. Yang got to “These past few days my heart has been far from calm,” and asked why this line was placed at the beginning and what job it did; she called on three people, and all three stumbled through answers. Then her eyes swept the classroom, swept to the row by the window, and stopped.

    Chen Xi wasn’t asleep. He was reading.

    The book was under the desk, open on his lap; he had his head down, mask pulled down under his chin, eyes fixed on the page. It was a very thick book with a dark blue cover, a few words printed on the spine that couldn’t be made out from the front.

    “Chen Xi.”

    Chen Xi looked up.

    “Stand up.”

    He stood up, the book still in his hand, forgetting to put it down.

    Ms. Yang came down from the platform, walked to his desk, pulled the book out of his hand, and turned it over to look at the cover.

    The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Volume III.

    “Quantum mechanics,” Ms. Yang read the small print on the spine, and looked up at him. “You’re in Year Ten, and you’re reading quantum mechanics?”

    “Yeah.”

    “Do you understand it?”

    “About half.”

    Someone in the class laughed out loud, and quickly covered their mask.

    Ms. Yang slapped the book down on his desk, smack, much louder than the physics teacher’s chalk.

    “You can understand quantum mechanics, but you can’t understand Zhu Ziqing?” She stuck out a finger and pointed it at Chen Xi’s nose, her voice under the mask shooting up. “Last term’s finals: maths out of a hundred and fifty, you got a hundred and forty-eight, physics full marks, chemistry full marks, Chinese out of a hundred and fifty, you got ninety-two! Ninety-two! My first day taking over this class I went through the results and when I got to you I thought it had been entered wrong. You tell me, is that acceptable?”

    “No.”

    “You know it’s not acceptable, and you’re reading this in my class?!”

    “I was listening,” said Chen Xi. “‘Far from calm’ at the beginning states the theme and sets the emotional tone of the whole piece; the lotus pond in the middle is to work off that unrest; the ending comes back to it, so the beginning and end echo each other.”

    Ms. Yang’s finger froze in mid-air.

    “…Then why didn’t you write that in the exam?”

    “In the exam I thought,” said Chen Xi, “he was just in a bad mood those few days.”

    This time the class couldn’t hold it in, and burst out laughing.

    Ms. Yang’s face flushed red, right up to the bit of forehead above her mask. She drew her finger back, took a deep breath and let it out, and her mask puffed out.

    “Sit down,” she said. “I’m confiscating the book. Come to my office after class to get it.”

    Chen Xi sat down.

    Ms. Yang carried the Feynman back to the platform, put it down there, and carried on with the lesson. A few sentences in, she glanced down at the book; it was open at a page covered in pencil marks, with a line of very small writing in the margin.

    She looked at the line once, didn’t understand it, and closed the book.

    After class, Chen Xi went to the office for the book. Ms. Yang handed it back to him, but didn’t let go straight away.

    “That essay of yours about the dog,” she said, “I read it.”

    Chen Xi was taken aback.

    That had been last term’s midterm essay; a different teacher had marked it, and Ms. Yang hadn’t taken over the class then.

    “At a teaching group meeting, someone brought it out and said this student’s central idea isn’t clear, there’s no elevation,” said Ms. Yang. “I read it.”

    “…”

    “It’s good,” said Ms. Yang. “You just can’t write like that in an exam.”

    She let go.

    “Exams need elevation,” she said. “Remember that: exams need elevation. After the exam, write however you like.”

    Chen Xi stood there holding the book.

    “Ms. Yang,” he said, “the dog died. Elevated into what?”

    Ms. Yang thought for a moment.

    “Into ‘from then on I understood,’” she said. “Understood anything you like. Understood life, understood how to treasure things, understood how wicked people can be. A marker reads several hundred essays a day; they don’t read what you wrote in the middle, they look at whether there’s an ‘I understood’ at the end.”

    Chen Xi looked at her for a while.

    “Isn’t that cheating.”

    “Yes,” said Ms. Yang. “Go to your lesson.”

    3. Evening Study

    Chen Xi’s classes moved to evening study.

    Not because he wanted to move them; there was no other way. Eight classes during the day, and after school, supper and then evening study, which ended at half past nine; by the time anyone got home it was past ten, and who was going to do an online class then? But that group of over a hundred people was still there, the problems still couldn’t be done, and the money was still wanted.

    So he taught during evening study.

    The method was simple. Evening study was for doing your own homework, and if there was something you couldn’t do, you could ask. The teacher on duty sat at the front marking, and didn’t usually bother with anything. Chen Xi sat in the row by the window; when someone brought over a paper to ask, he explained. When he’d explained, the person went back and carried on writing. Money wasn’t handed over in the classroom: there was a teacher on duty, and phones weren’t allowed—though everyone had one.

    He could get through a dozen or more people a night. People from Class Three and Class Eight slipped over too, standing at Class Seven’s back door, poking their heads in, waiting for him to finish one so the next could come in.

    The teacher on duty looked up a few times, and saw a group of students crowded round one student, holding papers, going through problems, maths and physics, very seriously, someone sometimes drawing a diagram with a pen on scrap paper. That’s a good thing, the teacher thought. And went back to marking.

    The money was transferred in the toilets.

    “You crafty little sod,” Ye Zhixing said when he heard.

    “I don’t take money in class,” said Chen Xi. “I take it in the toilets. The duty teacher isn’t in charge of the toilets.”

    4. Hiring

    The cat café reopened, and nobody came.

    That upstairs room, which before the epidemic was packed every afternoon, now got two or three customers in an afternoon, all middle-schoolers from nearby who dropped in after school to sit for a while, stroke the cats, order a drink, and left within the hour. Old Zhou was back, but the griddle barely got fired up a few times a day; most of the time he sat at the kitchen door in his mask looking at his phone, short videos, laughing to himself.

    Now and then there was a delivery order. Mostly omurice; on Meituan, Ye Zhixia had given it a picture of Rice Cake lying next to a plate of omurice, Rice Cake’s video was still being shared, and some people ordered delivery just for that picture. When the delivery rider came to pick up, he stood at the door, poked his head in, and asked: “Where’s the fat cat?”

    Rice Cake was on the windowsill, not moving. It had managed to lose a little weight now, it wasn’t quite as round, but people still called it the fat cat.

    Most of the time, the shop’s only customer was Gu Xuerong.

    She came after school and sat in her usual spot by the windowsill, laptop in her arms, testing games. Briquette lay at her feet. In front of her was a bottle of Coke, sometimes Sprite, sometimes iced tea. The bottle of mineral water Su Tang had bought with those two yuan, she had drunk, and kept the empty bottle on the windowsill, next to Rice Cake.

    Ye Zhixing had stopped going to school.

    Once the competition classes stopped, he asked Mr. Wu for long leave. Mr. Wu was silent on the phone for ages, then said the first round is in September, you be back before September, and if you come back and can’t do the problems any more, you’re no student of mine. So he worked full time at the shop, facing his computer from morning to night.

    The cats all liked to get close to him.

    When he sat, Rice Cake lay on his lap; when he stood, Calico rubbed his shins; when he lay on the sofa for a nap, the Devon burrowed into the hollow of his neck. Ye Zhixia said it was because he was warm: sitting still all day with a hot computer, he was like a heater himself.

    “I’m a cat tree and an electric heater,” said Ye Zhixing.

    “Very multi-functional.”

    The people were found at the end of April.

    He thought later it was probably because of the epidemic. In March he had interviewed nine people, and they were either too expensive or no good. In April he posted the jobs again on Town Matters and a few programmers’ forums, and suddenly lots of people came, of every kind.

    The first was called Ali, twenty-one, from Chengdu, freelancing from home, doing Cocos and Unity, with a dozen-odd mini-games in his portfolio, two of them doing well on WeChat. In the video interview Ye Zhixing saw someone with long hair on camera, wearing white cat-ear headphones and a pink-and-white sweater; when the voice came out, it was a man’s.

    “Hello, Mr. Ye,” said Ali. “Let me say up front, I usually dress in women’s clothes, and I might dress like this for meetings too. If you mind, let’s not waste each other’s time.”

    “What do you wear when you code?”

    “…This, too.”

    “Then that’s fine,” said Ye Zhixing. “I looked at your portfolio. The third one, the runner: did you write the collision detection yourself, or use the engine’s built-in one?”

    Ali stopped short, then laughed. “Wrote it myself. The built-in one drops frames on low-end Android phones.”

    “How much a month?”

    Ali named a figure. Half the Hangzhou man’s, a bit more than the Zhengzhou one’s.

    “Fine.”

    The second was a third-year computer science student at a university in Zhengzhou, called Meng Fan; his university was still doing online classes, so he had classes in the day and took on work at night, and said he wanted to build up some project experience before he graduated. He didn’t talk much, answered each question as it was asked, and answered precisely. Ye Zhixing set him a problem; he finished it in half an hour, and attached a note, which said “I used a rather clumsy method here, because you said it should be easy to maintain.”

    The third was a seventeen-year-old boy from Zhumadian who had dropped out in Year Eleven and taught himself to code at home for over a year; he had written a Flappy Bird clone where the bird was replaced by a duck his family kept. Ye Zhixing asked him why he had dropped out, and he said: “School’s useless, I want to make games.” Ye Zhixing asked whether his parents agreed, and he said: “No. I dropped out anyway.”

    “How old were you when you dropped out?”

    “Sixteen.”

    “And now seventeen?”

    “Yeah.”

    Ye Zhixing looked at the face on the screen. Very young, dark circles under the eyes, and on the wall behind him a yellowed certificate, “Merit Student,” dated 2012.

    He had Uncle He phone the boy’s family. When Uncle He came back he said the mother had cried on the phone, said as long as the child had something proper to do, the money didn’t matter, just don’t let him shut himself in his room playing games all day.

    “Juvenile worker,” said Uncle He. “Same rules. Medical, registration, no staying up all night.”

    “I know.”

    With more people, the work spread out.

    Rice Cake’s Diet went live at the start of April. In the first week it passed a thousand visitors and the ad programme switched on; in the second week, Rice Cake’s video was shared again by a big account, and visitors suddenly went up dozens of times over. Daily ad revenue went from a few dozen yuan to a few hundred, then from a few hundred to over a thousand.

    Big Liu and Huang Yingjun did the second game, Ali did the third on his own, Meng Fan the fourth, the boy from Zhumadian the fifth. Ye Zhixing wrote too. He had been learning from Big Liu for over a month; he wasn’t fast, and it wasn’t pretty, but he could do it. What he wrote was a very simple thing, a cat jumping along a row of squares, falling off if it jumped wrong, and the cat he drew was Briquette.

    Of the five games, two nobody played, and they were taken down. Three stayed, and with Rice Cake’s Diet that made four games, and the daily ad revenue from all of them together passed several thousand.

    That evening, Ye Zhixing took a screenshot of the numbers in the back end and looked at it for a good while.

    Then he leaned back in his chair and let out a long breath.

    Rice Cake rolled over on his lap and spread its belly out.

    He reached down and stroked Rice Cake’s belly, stroked it twice, then stopped, his hand resting there, not taking it away.

    Enough. For the next six months at least, enough.

    5. The Dorm

    Lin Xiaoman came back the day before term started.

    Her parents had gone back to Guangdong on the factory coach at the beginning of March, and she had stayed on in the village for over a month, living with her grandparents. The day before term, her grandpa drove her to the county town on his electric three-wheeler, the cargo bed holding her suitcase, a bag of rice, a bag of dried sweet potato her grandma had made, and an old hen in a woven sack, its head sticking out of the top of the sack, clucking the whole way.

    “For your dorm to make soup,” said her grandpa. “Build you up.”

    The dorm was the same dorm. The old residential block, third floor, twenty square metres, two sets of bunk beds. Of the other two roommates, one had changed schools, and one’s family wouldn’t let her come, saying the epidemic wasn’t over and she should stay home another term. That left Lin Xiaoman and Gu Xuerong.

    When Lin Xiaoman pushed the door open, Gu Xuerong was sitting on the lower bunk with her laptop in her arms and a bottle of Coke in front of her.

    The two of them looked at each other for a few seconds.

    “…Xuerong!”

    Lin Xiaoman flung her suitcase down and threw herself at her. She threw herself so fast she banged her knee on the edge of the bed, said “ow,” didn’t care, and hugged Gu Xuerong tight, so tight the laptop in Gu Xuerong’s arms nearly fell.

    “Long time no see long time no see long time no see!”

    “…Mm.”

    “Let me look at you.” Lin Xiaoman let go, stepped back, took Gu Xuerong’s face in her hands and looked left and right, then squeezed her arm, squeezed her shoulder. “You’ve put on weight! You really have! Your face is rounder! There’s meat on your arms!”

    Gu Xuerong looked down at her own arm.

    “…Is there.”

    “Yes! Before, when I squeezed you it was all bone, it hurt my hand!” said Lin Xiaoman. “Now it’s soft!”

    She squeezed once more, to check, and then her whole body relaxed, and she plonked down beside Gu Xuerong, the bed boards creaking.

    “I thought…” she said, “when I was in the village, I sent you messages every day, sometimes you answered, sometimes you didn’t. I was so scared you…” She didn’t finish. “Seeing you’re all right, I feel much better.”

    “I’m all right.”

    “Mm!” said Lin Xiaoman. “Whatever happens, don’t give up, OK?”

    Gu Xuerong looked at her.

    “Give up what?”

    “…Like,” Lin Xiaoman thought, “don’t give up anything.”

    “Oh.”

    That evening, Lin Xiaoman carried the old hen downstairs and begged the woman who ran the little shop on the ground floor to kill it for her, and stewed a pot of soup. The soup was very rich, with a layer of golden fat floating on top; Lin Xiaoman ladled a big bowl for Gu Xuerong and a big bowl for herself, and the two of them sat on the edge of the bed drinking it.

    “Xuerong, what are you playing lately?”

    “Testing games.”

    “Not testing, playing. For yourself. Anything fun?”

    Gu Xuerong thought. “There’s one where the main character is a little girl, in a big house, and the people in the house have no faces—”

    “Stop stop stop!” Lin Xiaoman covered her ears. “Is it scary? I don’t want to hear scary stuff!”

    “…MC, then.”

    “MC’s good! I like MC!” said Lin Xiaoman. “My little cousin plays it every day. I played in the village too, I built a chicken coop! But I can’t get the chickens to lay, they just stand there.”

    “Standing there is laying,” said Gu Xuerong. “Chickens in the game don’t need feeding, every few minutes they lay one by themselves, it drops on the ground, and you have to go and pick it up.”

    “What? Then I’ve never picked up a single one!”

    “Then under that coop of yours, by now, the ground should be covered in eggs.”

    Lin Xiaoman drank a mouthful of soup, so hot she had to suck in air.

    “School is so annoying,” she said. “That director from academic affairs today, did you hear him, no long hair, no long nails. I’d only just grown my nails, look—” She held out her hand; the nails had grown a little, painted a very pale clear coat. “I did them at home, and tomorrow I have to cut them. Gross.”

    “Mm.”

    “And no sleeping in class,” said Lin Xiaoman. “It’s not that I want to sleep, I can’t get up in the morning, I’m sleepy. In the village I got up at eight every day.”

    “Mm.”

    “And going on about expelling people all the time.” Lin Xiaoman put down her bowl, her voice dropping. “‘Anyone who doesn’t want to be here doesn’t have to be, there are plenty of people behind you who’d like to get in.’ When he said that, loads of people in our class looked down. And I thought, what if I get expelled. My mum and dad are still at the factory, they only come home once a year. If they found out…”

    Gu Xuerong looked at her.

    “You won’t get expelled.”

    “How do you know?”

    “You follow the rules,” said Gu Xuerong. “He said no long nails, and tomorrow you’ll cut them.”

    Lin Xiaoman spread her fingers and closed them again, and sighed.

    “…True.”

    She picked up her bowl again and drank some soup.

    “Xuerong, how are things with your family?” she asked. “Last time Chen Xi said you went to the mediation room…”

    “It’s fine now.”

    “Really fine?”

    “Mm. They don’t know where I live.”

    “And later?”

    Gu Xuerong didn’t answer.

    “I don’t know what we’re going to have to face later either,” said Lin Xiaoman. “Sometimes at night I think about it, and the more I think the less I can sleep. My grades are so bad, I won’t get into a good university, and later I’ll go to Guangdong and work in a factory, same as my mum and dad. It’s not that I think factory work is bad, it’s just… it’s like I can see right to the end.”

    “…”

    “What about you? Have you thought about later?”

    “No.”

    “Then you should,” said Lin Xiaoman. “You’re cleverer than me. Even Chen Xi says your physics has improved.”

    Gu Xuerong looked down at the layer of golden fat in her bowl.

    “I’ll think about it,” she said.

    Lin Xiaoman went to sleep at half past ten.

    Her routine was very regular now. A month and more in the village, in bed by half past nine every night along with her grandparents; back in the county town, she had brought the habit with her: wash at ten, in bed at ten-twenty, lights out at half past ten—the light being the little lamp at the head of her own bed—and she pulled the quilt over her head, said “night, Xuerong,” and within five minutes her breathing had slowed.

    Gu Xuerong was still awake.

    She sat on the lower bunk with her back against the wall, the laptop screen turned down to its lowest brightness, which was still a bit bright, so she pushed the laptop further under the quilt and used the quilt to block the glow. Earphones in.

    That afternoon Big Liu had posted a new build in the group, Meng Fan’s, a game about stacking blocks upward, where if the blocks went crooked they fell. She had played it for two hours and stacked up to level one hundred and forty-seven.

    On level one hundred and forty-seven, she discovered that if she switched to the background at the moment a block dropped and then switched back, the block hung in mid-air and didn’t fall. It just hung there. She stacked another on top, and that one hung too. She stacked another.

    She stacked thirty levels of floating blocks, and on the screen there was a thin, crooked column not touching the ground.

    She took a screenshot and wrote in the test report:

    7. From level 147, switching to the background at the moment a block drops and switching back leaves the block floating, unaffected by gravity. You can keep stacking up and it won’t fall. I stacked 30 levels. No crash. Suggest fixing it. (Not fixing it is fine too, it looks nice)

    When she’d written it, she glanced at the time. One twenty-two.

    Eight minutes left.

    On the top bunk, Lin Xiaoman rolled over and mumbled something too faint to make out; it sounded like “the chicken laid an egg.”

    6. Sunday Afternoon

    There were no classes on Sunday afternoon.

    It was the only half day off in the week. Chen Xi slipped away straight after lunch, didn’t go home, went straight to the cat café. Su Tang didn’t have to do customer service in the afternoon—customer service had moved to the evenings, seven to eleven; evening study was voluntary, and she had simply stopped going—so she came too, carrying a bag of fried dough twists her mum had made. Ye Zhixia was at school; Year Nine had make-up classes on Sunday afternoons too. Gu Xuerong was there already, in her usual spot by the windowsill.

    Four people, eleven cats.

    Chen Xi lay down on the sofa the moment he came in, put his feet up on the armrest, took the Feynman out of his schoolbag, opened it, and laid it over his face.

    “Ms. Yang gave it back?” Su Tang asked.

    “Yep.” Chen Xi’s voice came out from under the book, muffled. “And told me exams need elevation.”

    “Elevation?”

    “Writing ‘from then on I understood’ at the end.”

    Su Tang let out a “pfft” of laughter. “So did you understand?”

    “I understood that Chinese teachers have a hard time too.”

    Ye Zhixing was writing code behind the bar counter. He wrote very slowly: a few lines, stop, look something up, a few more lines. Briquette jumped up on the counter and lay down beside his keyboard, and its tail swept across the touchpad, and the code on the screen shot down to the very bottom.

    “…Briquette.”

    Briquette yawned.

    “It’s helping you,” said Gu Xuerong without looking up.

    “Helping me with what?”

    “That bit you wrote is wrong. Scroll down and you can’t see it.”

    Ye Zhixing scrolled the code back up and looked. It really was wrong.

    “…How do you know?”

    “You stopped three times just now,” said Gu Xuerong. “Every time on the same line.”

    Chen Xi lifted the book off his face, looked at Gu Xuerong, then at Ye Zhixing, and put the book back.

    Later Ye Zhixing stopped coding, shut the laptop, came over, and sat down at the other end of the sofa. Chen Xi pulled his feet back to make room for him.

    “Heard you found people?” Chen Xi lifted the book halfway off his face. “Weren’t you crossing out names last month till your pen ran dry?”

    “Found them, three,” said Ye Zhixing. “Last month everyone still thought this would be over in a couple of weeks, they were all playing it cool, twenty-five thousand the moment they opened their mouths. This month they’ve all worked it out: it’s not ending, they can’t go back to the big cities, they don’t dare go out on their own, so if they can get some work at home they’ll take it, whatever it pays, nobody’s picky any more.” He paused. “So now it’s my turn to be picky.”

    Chen Xi took the book right off and turned his head to look at him.

    “You sound like a capitalist.”

    “I am one. High-school capitalist, a county-town speciality, can’t get them anywhere else.”

    Chen Xi looked at him for a few seconds, and didn’t laugh.

    “Hey, seriously,” he said. “I think you’ve been pretty down lately. Back at military training you were joking around, even standing at attention you had to talk back to the instructor, got five laps and asked him if that was enough. Now every day you just sit there facing your computer, not one word of nonsense, like a time clock. Look at those dark circles, people will think you got beaten up.”

    Ye Zhixing didn’t answer straight away. Rice Cake jumped down from the windowsill, came over to his feet, rubbed once, and jumped onto his lap, and he gathered it up.

    “I’m scared,” he said.

    “Of what?”

    “Of Rice Cake’s diet failing,” said Ye Zhixing. “If it doesn’t slim down, my game is false advertising, someone’ll report it.”

    Chen Xi clicked his tongue, threw the book onto the coffee table, and sat up.

    “Big boss Ye, don’t give me that,” he said. “Whatever mistake you made before, I don’t know, you haven’t said, and I can’t be bothered to ask. All I know is you’re sixteen this year, same as me. A high-school kid, not some immortal, piling everything onto yourself, can you even carry it all? If you can’t, just give a shout, shouting isn’t shameful, I won’t charge you for it.”

    He grinned.

    “Stop showing off, bro.”

    Ye Zhixing looked down, stroking Rice Cake’s back, stroked it for a good while before he laughed.

    “You,” he said, “all these lines, so how come you only got ninety-two in Chinese?”

    “Ms. Yang would like to know too.”

    Su Tang had been sitting at the bar counter all along, not joining in, holding a dough twist, holding it for ages without eating it.

    “The things you were saying…” she began, “the future and stuff, big cities and stuff, capitalists and stuff. I don’t really get them.”

    All three of them looked at her.

    Her face was a bit red, but she didn’t stop.

    “I just think,” she said, “making everyone happy, that’s the most important thing, isn’t it? My dream is actually really simple, it’s to make my mum and dad happy, and make my friends happy.” She paused, and laughed again. “And I’ve got loads of friends, you know. Half of Class Three are my friends.”

    “Half?” said Chen Xi.

    “Half! Go and ask if you don’t believe me!”

    “I didn’t say I don’t believe you.”

    “It’s written on your face that you don’t.”

    “Who did you learn that one from?”

    “Ye Zhixing,” said Su Tang. “He learned it from Xuerong.”

    Over by the windowsill, Gu Xuerong’s hand on the mouse paused, then carried on clicking.

    Su Tang turned to look at Ye Zhixing.

    “I don’t really understand what you talk about,” she said. “But if you want to tell me, I’ll listen. If you don’t want to, never mind. I’m not going to force you.” She held out the dough twist in her hand. “Cheer up. Look, I’m always working hard too.”

    Ye Zhixing took the dough twist.

    “Working hard at what?”

    “Working hard at customer service! Working hard at not dropping out of the top fifty! Working hard at learning Yu’e Bao!” Su Tang counted on her fingers. “I know now, the money in Yu’e Bao goes into a fund, and the fund uses it to buy… to buy that…”

    “Money-market instruments.”

    “Yes! That!”

    Ye Zhixing bit into the dough twist. It was fried very crisp, and cracked when he bit it, crumbs falling all over Rice Cake. Rice Cake shook its fur and didn’t leave.

    Later Chen Xi went over to the windowsill to see what Gu Xuerong was testing.

    Gu Xuerong had two windows open on her screen. One was Meng Fan’s block-stacking game, blocks hanging in mid-air, a thin column. The other was a picture, very large, black background, packed with tiny figures, some in pots of oil, some tied to posts, some being sawn from the top of the head downward by two green-faced, fanged things, the sawn places drawn with red lines, one after another.

    “…What the hell is that?”

    “The transformations of hell,” said Gu Xuerong. “Found it online. Same version as the one she stuck up in the kitchen.”

    Chen Xi looked at the picture once, looked again, then turned his face away.

    “Don’t show me that!” he said. “I’ll have nightmares!”

    “You can understand quantum mechanics.”

    “Quantum mechanics doesn’t saw people in half!”

    Su Tang came over, glanced at the screen, cried “ah,” and covered her eyes.

    “That’s… that’s the one you said? On the wall across from your bed?”

    “Mm.”

    Chen Xi turned round and looked at Su Tang, then at Gu Xuerong.

    “What, across from the bed?”

    Su Tang glanced at Gu Xuerong. Gu Xuerong said nothing, which counted as yes. So Su Tang, quietly, picked out a few things from what she had heard that day in the basement: the kitchen, this picture, three years, karmic creditors, the debt-collecting kind, not allowed medicine for a fever, kneeling to listen to chanting.

    As Chen Xi listened, the expression on his face changed bit by bit.

    “…For real?” he said. “What kind of animals are your parents?”

    Gu Xuerong closed the window with the picture.

    Ye Zhixing sat on the sofa holding Rice Cake, and hadn’t made a sound all this time. When Chen Xi had said that, he spoke.

    “The stuff she plays,” he said, “really is insane.”

    Chen Xi looked back at him.

    “The first time I watched that anime she recommended, I got to episode nine and threw up,” said Ye Zhixing. “At the time I thought, what kind of person can watch this without blinking.” He stroked Rice Cake. “Now I know.”

    “…”

    “Those parents of hers,” said Ye Zhixing, “are animals.”

    The room went quiet for a moment. At the kitchen door, Old Zhou in his mask had a short video playing halfway through, someone in it shouting “family!”, and Old Zhou quickly turned the sound off.

    “Right, right.” Su Tang clapped her hands. “Enough of that! Eat the dough twists! My mum fried a whole bag, nobody leaves till they’re gone!”

    Towards evening, Su Tang had to go back; customer service started at seven. As she was packing her things, her phone pinged: an alert from the customer-service back end, a new message.

    She opened it.

    It was the woman from the noodle shop across from the county hospital.

    young lady!!! we can do dine-in today!!!
    my bone broth is on again!!!
    come for noodles when youre free!! my treat!!!

    After it came a photo: a big iron pot, milky white broth in it, giving off great clouds of steam that had fogged up half the lens.

    Su Tang held up her phone and showed everyone.

    “Look look!”

    Chen Xi glanced at it: “Oh.”

    Ye Zhixing glanced at it: “Good news.”

    Gu Xuerong glanced at it and asked: “How much is a bowl of noodles?”

    “She says it’s her treat!”

    “Then take me.”

    Su Tang was taken aback for a moment, then laughed.

    “OK!”
